chapters.n: Luke opens his second volume by addressing Theophilus again. His “former treatise” — the Gospel of Luke — told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what the risen Lord continued doing through his apostles and the Holy Ghost.

f.g: treatise = a written account.
Greek for “friend of God” or “loved by God”; probably a real patron, perhaps a Roman official.

chapters.n: The Gospel ran until Jesus was taken up to heaven, after he had instructed his chosen apostles through the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the apostles whom he had chosen

chapters.n: After his suffering, Jesus proved he was alive with many convincing evidences, appearing to them over forty days and teaching about God’s kingdom.

f.g: passion = suffering, especially Christ’s suffering and death.
Forty is a biblical number of preparation.

chapters.n: While eating with them, he commanded them to stay in Jerusalem and wait for what the Father had promised — the gift of the Holy Ghost.
John baptized with water, but in a few days they would be baptized with the Holy Ghost. Latter-day Saints see these as two parts of one baptism — of water and of the Spirit.
The apostles ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel — still hoping for national, political deliverance.

f.w: restore again the kingdom to Israel

chapters.n: Jesus replies that the timing of such events is the Father’s business, not theirs to know.

Instead they will receive power when the Holy Ghost comes, and be his witnesses in widening circles — Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. This verse outlines the whole book of Acts.

f.w: ye shall be witnesses unto me
unto the uttermost part of the earth

chapters.n: As they watch, he is lifted up and a cloud hides him from view. Clouds often signal God’s presence in scripture.

f.w: a cloud received him out of their sight

chapters.n: While they stare into the sky, two men in white — angels — appear beside them.

f.w: two men stood by them in white apparel

chapters.n: The angels ask why the Galileans stand gazing upward: this same Jesus will return in the same way they saw him go. His Second Coming will be personal, visible, and glorious.

f.w: shall so come in like manner

chapters.n: They return to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, a short walk — about two-thirds of a mile.

f.g: The distance the rabbis allowed one to walk on the Sabbath: about 2,000 cubits, roughly 0.6 miles (1 km).
Olivet = the Mount of Olives.

chapters.n: They go to the upper room where they are staying. Luke lists the eleven remaining apostles — the Twelve minus Judas Iscariot.

f.g: “The Zealot,” possibly once part of a movement zealous for Jewish independence.
Probably the same as Thaddeus (Matthew 10:3).

chapters.n: They all pray together with one heart — along with faithful women, Mary the mother of Jesus (her last mention in the Bible), and Jesus’s brothers, who now believe.

f.g: with one accord = united in mind and purpose.

chapters.n: During those days Peter, now leading, stands up among about 120 believers.
Peter says scripture spoken by the Holy Ghost through David had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus.

f.g: must needs = had to.

chapters.n: Judas had been one of them, sharing in their ministry — which makes his fall all the more tragic.

Luke adds a parenthetical note on Judas’s grim end: the field bought with his betrayal money became the place where he fell and his body burst open. Matthew says Judas hanged himself; many readers harmonize the two accounts by supposing his body later fell.

f.g: asunder = apart.

chapters.n: Everyone in Jerusalem knew of it, and the field was called Akeldama, “Field of Blood,” in their local Aramaic.

f.g: Aramaic ḥaqel dema, “field of blood.”

chapters.n: Peter quotes two Psalms: one about the betrayer’s home becoming deserted, and one about another taking his office.

f.g: bishoprick = office or position of oversight.

chapters.n: So a replacement must come from those who had been with them throughout the Lord’s ministry.

f.g: companied = kept company, traveled together.

chapters.n: The replacement must have been with them from John’s baptism to the Ascension, to be ordained as a witness of the Resurrection — the core of an apostle’s calling.

f.w: a witness with us of his resurrection

chapters.n: They put forward two candidates: Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias.

f.g: A Latin name meaning “just, righteous.” Using multiple names was common.

chapters.n: They pray to the Lord, who knows every heart, asking him to show which one he has chosen. The choice is the Lord’s, not theirs.

f.w: which knowest the hearts of all men
shew whether of these two thou hast chosen

chapters.n: The chosen one will take the place in the apostolic ministry that Judas abandoned through transgression to go “to his own place.”

f.g: A sober phrase for the destiny Judas chose for himself.

chapters.n: They cast lots, and the lot falls to Matthias, who is added to the eleven. The Quorum of the Twelve is kept full — a pattern Latter-day Saints see continued in the restored Church.

f.g: Casting lots was a traditional way of seeking God’s decision; it is never used again after the Spirit is poured out.

chapters.n: Pentecost arrives — fifty days after Passover — and the believers are gathered together in one place, united in heart.

f.g: Greek for “fiftieth.” Also called the Feast of Weeks, a harvest festival; Jewish tradition later linked it to the giving of the law at Sinai.

chapters.n: Suddenly a sound like a roaring wind fills the house. In both Hebrew and Greek, the same word can mean wind, breath, and spirit.
Flames like divided tongues of fire appear and rest on each of them. Fire symbolizes God’s presence and the purifying power of the Spirit.

f.w: cloven tongues like as of fire
f.g: cloven = divided, split.

chapters.n: All are filled with the Holy Ghost and begin speaking in other languages as the Spirit enables them. The promised baptism of the Spirit has come.
Jerusalem is crowded with devout Jews from all over the world who had come for the festival or settled in the city.

f.w: out of every nation under heaven
f.g: Jews of the Diaspora, scattered across the Roman and Parthian empires.

chapters.n: Hearing the commotion, a crowd gathers and is bewildered: each one hears the disciples speaking in his own native language.

f.g: noised abroad = reported widely.
The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for the confusion at Babel; Pentecost reverses Babel.

chapters.n: Amazed, they ask whether these speakers aren’t all Galileans — unschooled country folk with a recognizable accent.

f.g: Galileans had a distinctive accent.

chapters.n: How can each of them hear their own mother tongue?

f.g: Their native language, learned from birth.

chapters.n: Luke lists the peoples present, moving roughly from east to west: Parthians, Medes, Elamites (modern Iran), Mesopotamia (Iraq), Judea, and regions of Asia Minor (Turkey).

f.g: Descendants of Jews exiled east centuries earlier by Assyria and Babylon.
Here the Roman province in western Asia Minor, not the continent.

chapters.n: The list continues across Asia Minor, North Africa, and even Rome — both Jews by birth and proselytes, Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

f.g: A city in modern Libya.
proselytes = converts to Judaism.
Visitors from Rome.

chapters.n: Cretans and Arabs complete the list. All hear the disciples declaring God’s mighty works in their own languages. The gospel is for every nation.

f.g: People of the island of Crete.

chapters.n: Everyone is astonished and perplexed, asking what it means.

f.g: were in doubt = were perplexed, at a loss.

chapters.n: Others sneer that the disciples are simply drunk.

f.g: Sweet new wine — a mocking dismissal.

chapters.n: Peter stands with the other eleven apostles and boldly addresses the crowd — the same Peter who denied Jesus weeks earlier, now transformed by the Holy Ghost.

f.w: Peter, standing up with the eleven

f.g: hearken = listen carefully.

chapters.n: These men aren’t drunk, he says with a touch of humor — it’s only nine in the morning.

f.w: the third hour of the day
f.g: About 9 a.m., the hour of morning prayer and sacrifice.

chapters.n: Instead, this is what the prophet Joel foretold.

f.g: When Moroni appeared to Joseph Smith, he quoted this same passage from Joel and said it was not yet fulfilled but soon would be.

chapters.n: Peter quotes Joel: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all people. Sons and daughters will prophesy, young men see visions, old men dream dreams — the Spirit is not limited by age or gender.

f.w: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh
your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

chapters.n: Even servants and handmaids — the lowest in society — will receive the Spirit and prophesy.

f.g: handmaidens = female servants.

chapters.n: Joel’s prophecy continues with signs in the heavens and on earth: blood, fire, and smoke — imagery of God’s coming judgment.
The sun will darken and the moon turn to blood before the great day of the Lord. Peter sees the last days as having begun, with fuller fulfillment still ahead.

f.w: The sun shall be turned into darkness

f.g: notable = glorious, conspicuous.

chapters.n: And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Peter is about to show that “the Lord” is Jesus.

f.w: whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved

chapters.n: Peter now turns to Jesus of Nazareth: God endorsed him publicly through miracles, wonders, and signs that they themselves witnessed.

f.g: approved = attested, shown to be genuine.

chapters.n: Jesus was handed over according to God’s set plan and foreknowledge — yet they are still responsible for crucifying him through lawless hands. God’s plan doesn’t erase human accountability.

f.w: the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God

f.g: Literally “lawless hands” — likely the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

chapters.n: But God raised him up, freeing him from death’s agony, because death could not possibly keep its hold on him.

f.g: holden = held.

chapters.n: Peter cites David in Psalm 16: “I saw the Lord always before me; he is at my right hand so I will not be shaken.”
So the psalmist’s heart rejoices and his body rests in hope.

f.w: my flesh shall rest in hope

chapters.n: God will not abandon his soul to the realm of the dead nor let his Holy One see decay. “Hell” here means the world of spirits, not the place of punishment.

f.g: Greek hadēs, Hebrew sheol — the abode of the dead.
corruption = bodily decay.

chapters.n: God has shown him the paths of life and will fill him with joy in his presence.

f.g: countenance = face, presence.

chapters.n: Peter argues plainly: David died, was buried, and his tomb is still in Jerusalem. So he wasn’t speaking of himself.

f.w: his sepulchre is with us unto this day

chapters.n: David was a prophet who knew God had sworn an oath to put one of his descendants on his throne — the Messiah.

f.w: God had sworn with an oath to him

chapters.n: Foreseeing this, David spoke of the Messiah’s resurrection: not left among the dead, his body not decaying.
God raised this Jesus — and all the apostles are eyewitnesses. This is the heart of their testimony.
Exalted to God’s right hand, Jesus received the promised Holy Ghost from the Father and has poured out what they now see and hear.

f.w: by the right hand of God exalted

f.g: shed forth = poured out.

chapters.n: David did not ascend to heaven, yet he wrote in Psalm 110: “The LORD said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.”

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord
f.g: “LORD” in capitals stands for the divine name; Peter applies “my Lord” to the exalted Christ.

chapters.n: …until God makes his enemies a footstool for his feet — a picture of total victory.

f.g: Conquerors sometimes placed their feet on defeated enemies’ necks.

chapters.n: Peter’s conclusion: all Israel should know for certain that God has made this Jesus — whom they crucified — both Lord and Messiah.
Cut to the heart, the listeners ask the apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?” Real conviction leads to a desire to change.

Peter answers clearly: repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. These are the first principles and ordinances of the gospel.

f.w: Repent, and be baptized every one of you
f.r: Articles of Faith 1:4; 3 Nephi 27:20; 2 Nephi 31:17; D&C 49:13-14

f.g: remission = forgiveness, cancellation of a debt.

chapters.n: The promise is for them, their children, and those far away — everyone the Lord calls. It reaches across generations and nations.

f.w: to all that are afar off

chapters.n: With many more words Peter testifies and urges them to save themselves from this crooked generation.

f.g: untoward = crooked, perverse.

chapters.n: Those who gladly accept his message are baptized — about three thousand that day. At Sinai, tradition recalls, three thousand died (Exodus 32:28); at Pentecost, three thousand receive new life.
The new converts devote themselves to four things: the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking bread together (likely including the sacrament), and prayer.
A sense of awe settles on everyone as the apostles perform many wonders and signs.

f.g: Here reverent awe, not terror.

chapters.n: The believers stay together and share everything they own.
They sell property and possessions and distribute to anyone in need — an early form of the law of consecration.
Every day they worship together at the temple and share meals in homes with glad, sincere hearts. Early Christians still saw themselves as faithful Jews.

f.g: Simplicity, sincerity, undivided devotion.
Or “at home” — in private homes, the first Christian meeting places.

chapters.n: Praising God and respected by the people, they see the Lord add new believers every day. Growth is credited to the Lord, not to clever methods.

f.w: the Lord added to the church daily

chapters.n: Peter and John go up to the temple at three in the afternoon, a set time of prayer. The apostles keep worshipping at the temple as faithful Jews.

f.g: About 3 p.m., the time of the evening sacrifice and prayer.

chapters.n: A man unable to walk from birth is carried every day to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he begs from worshippers.

f.g: Over forty years old (Acts 4:22), with no hope of a cure.
Probably the ornate bronze Nicanor Gate on the east side of the temple courts.
alms = gifts of money to the poor.

chapters.n: Seeing Peter and John about to enter, he asks them for money.
Peter looks intently at him, together with John, and says, “Look at us.” They give him their full attention.

f.g: Gazing intently — a recurring phrase in Luke’s writings.

chapters.n: The man looks up, expecting a coin.

f.g: gave heed = paid attention.

chapters.n: Peter has no money, but offers what he does have — the power of Christ’s name: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk.”

f.w: Silver and gold have I none
In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth

chapters.n: Peter takes his right hand and lifts him up, and at once his feet and ankles grow strong.

f.w: he took him by the right hand

chapters.n: He leaps to his feet, walks, and goes into the temple with them — walking, jumping, and praising God. A man once kept outside now enters God’s house.

f.g: Isaiah foretold that in the messianic age “the lame man [shall] leap as an hart.”

chapters.n: Everyone sees him walking and praising God.

f.g: A public, undeniable miracle (see Acts 4:16).

chapters.n: They recognize him as the beggar from the Beautiful Gate and are filled with wonder at what happened.
Clinging to Peter and John, the healed man draws a crowd that comes running to Solomon’s Porch, astonished.

f.w: the porch that is called Solomon's
f.g: A covered colonnade along the east side of the temple’s outer court.

chapters.n: Peter seizes the moment: why are they amazed, and why stare at the apostles as if their own power or holiness did this?

f.w: as though by our own power or holiness

chapters.n: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has glorified his servant Jesus — the one they handed over and rejected before Pilate, even when Pilate wanted to release him.

f.w: The God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob

f.g: Greek pais, “servant” or “child” — likely echoing Isaiah’s Servant of the Lord (Isaiah 52:13).

f.w: when he was determined to let him go

chapters.n: They rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be released instead.

f.w: the Holy One and the Just

chapters.n: They killed the very Author of life — a stunning paradox — but God raised him from the dead, and the apostles are witnesses.

f.g: Greek archēgos — originator, pioneer, author. Hebrews 12:2 uses the same word.

chapters.n: It is Jesus’s name, through faith in that name, that has made this man completely whole in front of them all.

f.g: Complete health in every part.

chapters.n: Peter softens: he knows they and their leaders acted in ignorance.

f.g: wot = know.

chapters.n: God used even their actions to fulfill what all the prophets foretold: that the Messiah would suffer.
So repent and turn back to God so their sins may be wiped away, and times of refreshing may come from the Lord’s presence.

f.g: converted = turned around, turned back to God.
A period of spiritual renewal and rest given by God.

chapters.n: And God will send the Messiah appointed for them — Jesus — at his return.

Heaven must hold Jesus until the time of the restoration of all things foretold by the prophets. Latter-day Saints see this as pointing to the latter-day Restoration of the gospel before the Second Coming.

f.w: the times of restitution of all things
f.g: restitution = restoration.

chapters.n: Moses foretold that God would raise up a prophet like him, whom the people must heed. Jesus himself identified himself as that prophet, and Moroni quoted these words to Joseph Smith.

f.w: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you

chapters.n: Anyone who refuses to listen to that prophet will be cut off from God’s people.

f.w: shall be destroyed from among the people

chapters.n: Every prophet from Samuel onward also foretold these days.

f.g: Samuel anointed David, from whose line the Messiah would come.

chapters.n: They are heirs of the prophets and of God’s covenant with Abraham: through his seed all families of the earth will be blessed.

f.w: in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: God sent his risen Servant to them first, to bless them by turning each of them from their wickedness. The gospel went to Israel first, then to the Gentiles.

f.w: in turning away every one of you from his iniquities

chapters.n: While Peter and John are still speaking, the priests, the captain of the temple guard, and the Sadducees confront them.

f.g: The officer in charge of the temple police, second only to the high priest in temple authority.
A priestly, aristocratic party that rejected the resurrection and angels.

chapters.n: They are irritated that the apostles are teaching the people and proclaiming resurrection from the dead through Jesus — a direct challenge to Sadducee beliefs.

f.g: grieved = greatly annoyed, disturbed.

chapters.n: They arrest Peter and John and jail them overnight, since it is already evening.

f.g: in hold = in custody.
eventide = evening.

chapters.n: Yet many who heard believed, and the number of men in the movement grows to about five thousand. Arrests can’t stop the word.
The next day the Jewish leadership assembles — rulers, elders, and scribes.

f.g: The three groups making up the Sanhedrin.

chapters.n: The high priestly family is present: Annas, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and others — the same men who condemned Jesus.

f.w: Annas the high priest, and Caiaphas

chapters.n: Placing the apostles in the center, they demand: by what power or in whose name did you do this?

f.g: A name stood for authority — whom do you represent?

chapters.n: Filled with the Holy Ghost, Peter addresses the council respectfully. Jesus had promised the Spirit would give them words in such moments.
If they are on trial for doing a kindness to a disabled man and want to know how he was healed…

f.g: impotent = powerless, disabled.
Peter notes the irony of being tried for an act of kindness.

chapters.n: …let everyone know: it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth — whom they crucified and God raised — that this man stands before them healed.

f.w: whom ye crucified, whom God raised from the dead

chapters.n: Jesus is the stone the builders rejected that has become the cornerstone. The “builders” — Israel’s leaders — are sitting right in front of Peter.

f.w: the stone which was set at nought of you builders
f.g: set at nought = treated as worthless.
The cornerstone that aligns and supports the whole building.

chapters.n: Salvation is found in no one else; there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved — a central declaration of Christian faith echoed in the Book of Mormon.
The leaders are amazed at the boldness of these untrained fishermen and realize they had been with Jesus. Time with the Lord had changed them.

f.g: Without formal rabbinic training; “ignorant” means ordinary, laymen — not stupid.

chapters.n: With the healed man standing right there, they have no rebuttal.

f.w: they could say nothing against it

chapters.n: They send the apostles out of the room and confer privately.

f.g: Luke may have learned of the private discussion from a sympathizer like Paul, once a Pharisee, or another council member.

chapters.n: They admit the obvious: a remarkable miracle has been done, all Jerusalem knows it, and they can’t deny it.
Rather than respond to the evidence, they decide to threaten the apostles severely so the movement spreads no further.

f.g: straitly = strictly, severely.

chapters.n: They call them back and order them not to speak or teach at all in Jesus’s name.

f.w: commanded them not to speak at all

chapters.n: Peter and John reply: you judge whether it is right before God to obey you rather than God.

f.w: hearken unto you more than unto God

chapters.n: They simply cannot stop speaking about what they have seen and heard. True witnesses can’t keep silent.

f.w: we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard

chapters.n: After more threats, the council releases them, unable to find a way to punish them without angering the people, who are praising God.
Luke notes the healed man was over forty — a lifelong condition, making the miracle all the more striking.

f.g: A detail that underlines the impossibility of a natural recovery.

chapters.n: Released, they return to their fellow believers and report everything the leaders said.

f.g: Their fellow disciples, the believing community.

chapters.n: Hearing it, the believers pray together with one voice to the sovereign Creator of heaven, earth, and sea.

f.w: thou art God, which hast made heaven, and earth, and the sea

chapters.n: They quote Psalm 2, spoken through David: why do the nations rage and peoples plot in vain?

f.g: heathen = nations, Gentiles; vain = empty, futile.

chapters.n: The kings and rulers of earth gathered against the Lord and his Anointed — his Messiah.

f.g: Christ = the Anointed One, Hebrew Messiah.

chapters.n: They see the psalm fulfilled: Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all united against God’s holy servant Jesus.

f.g: child = servant (Greek pais), as in Acts 3:13.

chapters.n: Yet they only accomplished what God had already determined would happen. God’s purposes prevail even through his enemies’ actions.

f.w: thy hand and thy counsel determined before

chapters.n: They don’t pray for safety or for the threats to stop — they ask for boldness to keep speaking God’s word.

f.w: with all boldness they may speak thy word

chapters.n: And they ask God to keep stretching out his hand to heal and perform signs through Jesus’s name.
When they finish praying, the building shakes, they are all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they speak God’s word boldly. Their prayer is answered immediately.

f.w: spake the word of God with boldness

chapters.n: The believers are united in heart and soul. No one claims private ownership of possessions; they share everything.

f.w: of one heart and of one soul

chapters.n: With great power the apostles testify of the Lord Jesus’s resurrection, and God’s abundant grace rests on them all.

f.w: gave the apostles witness of the resurrection

chapters.n: No one among them is in need, because those who own land or houses sell them and bring the money — fulfilling the ideal of Deuteronomy that there be no poor among them.

f.w: Neither was there any among them that lacked

chapters.n: They lay the money at the apostles’ feet, and it is distributed to each as they need. Laying something at someone’s feet signaled giving it into their authority.

f.w: laid them down at the apostles' feet

chapters.n: Luke introduces Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, “son of encouragement.” He will become an important missionary companion of Paul.

f.g: consolation = comfort, encouragement, exhortation.
From the tribe of Levi, which traditionally served in temple duties.

chapters.n: Barnabas sells a field he owns and lays the money at the apostles’ feet — a model of generous consecration that sets up the contrasting story that follows.
In contrast to Barnabas, a couple named Ananias and Sapphira also sell some property.

f.g: Hebrew Hananiah, “the Lord is gracious” — an ironic name given the story.
The word links this story to Barnabas’s generous gift in Acts 4:36-37.

chapters.n: With his wife’s full knowledge, Ananias secretly keeps part of the money and presents the rest as if it were the whole amount. Their sin is not keeping money but pretending.

f.g: The same rare Greek verb describes Achan’s theft of devoted things in Joshua 7:1 (Greek Old Testament).
privy = secretly aware of, in on it.

chapters.n: Peter, discerning by the Spirit, asks why Ananias let Satan fill his heart to lie to the Holy Ghost by holding back part of the price.

f.w: to lie to the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: The land was his to keep, and the money was his to use. Giving was voluntary. His real offense was deception — lying not to men but to God. Note that lying to the Holy Ghost is called lying to God.

f.g: Consecration in the early Church was freely chosen, not forced.

f.w: thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God

chapters.n: Hearing this, Ananias collapses and dies. Great fear grips everyone who hears about it.

f.g: died.
Deep reverence and awe for the holiness of God.

chapters.n: Young men wrap the body and carry him out for burial. Burial typically took place the same day in that climate.

f.g: Wrapped the body in cloth for burial.

chapters.n: About three hours later his wife comes in, unaware of what has happened.

f.g: space = period of time.

chapters.n: Peter gives her a chance to tell the truth, asking if they sold the land for this amount. She says yes — repeating the lie.

f.w: Tell me whether ye sold the land for so much?
f.g: Peter’s question offers her an opportunity to be honest.

chapters.n: Peter asks how they could agree together to test the Spirit of the Lord. The men who buried her husband are at the door and will carry her out too.

f.w: tempt the Spirit of the Lord
f.g: tempt = put to the test, see how much one can get away with.

chapters.n: She falls at his feet and dies, and the young men bury her beside her husband.

f.g: died.

chapters.n: Great fear comes on the whole church and all who hear. This is Luke’s first use of the word “church” — a community set apart as holy, where God is not mocked.

f.g: Greek ekklēsia — an assembly “called out,” used in the Greek Old Testament for Israel’s congregation.

chapters.n: The apostles perform many signs and wonders among the people, and the believers regularly gather together in Solomon’s Porch at the temple.
Outsiders don’t dare join them casually, though the people hold them in high esteem.

f.g: durst = dared.
magnified = praised, held in high regard.

chapters.n: Still, more and more believers — crowds of men and women — are added to the Lord.

f.w: multitudes both of men and women

chapters.n: People carry the sick into the streets on cots and mats, hoping even Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passes.
Crowds also come from towns around Jerusalem bringing the sick and those troubled by evil spirits, and all are healed.

f.g: vexed = tormented.

chapters.n: The high priest and his Sadducee allies are filled with jealousy.

f.g: Greek zēlos — jealousy, envy.

chapters.n: They arrest the apostles and put them in the public jail.

f.g: The public jail.

chapters.n: But during the night an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors and leads them out.
The angel commands them to go stand in the temple and tell the people the full message of this new life.

f.w: all the words of this life

chapters.n: At dawn they are teaching in the temple. Meanwhile the high priest convenes the full Sanhedrin and the council of elders, and sends for the prisoners.

f.w: all the senate of the children of Israel
f.g: The full body of Israel’s elders.

chapters.n: The officers come back without them.

f.w: found them not in the prison
f.g: A touch of humor in Luke’s storytelling.

chapters.n: They report that the jail was securely locked and the guards were at their posts — but no one was inside.

f.w: the keepers standing without before the doors
f.g: keepers = guards; without = outside.

chapters.n: The leaders are baffled, wondering where this will lead.

f.w: they doubted of them whereunto this would grow
f.g: They were perplexed about what this would come to.

chapters.n: Then someone reports that the men they jailed are standing in the temple, teaching the people.

f.w: standing in the temple, and teaching

chapters.n: The captain and officers bring them in without force, fearing the crowd might stone them.

f.g: The leaders feared the people more than the apostles feared the leaders.

chapters.n: They stand the apostles before the council for questioning by the high priest.

He reminds them of the strict order not to teach in “this name” — refusing even to say Jesus’s name — and accuses them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and blaming the leaders for Jesus’s death.

f.w: bring this man's blood upon us

f.g: straitly = strictly.

chapters.n: Peter and the apostles give a clear principle: we must obey God rather than men.

f.w: We ought to obey God rather than men

chapters.n: The God of their ancestors raised up Jesus, whom the leaders killed by hanging him on a tree — a phrase recalling the law’s curse on one hanged on a tree.
God exalted him to his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give Israel repentance and forgiveness. Even repentance is a gift from Christ.
The apostles are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Ghost, whom God gives to those who obey him. Human and divine testimony stand together.

f.w: so is also the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Enraged, the council wants to kill them.

f.g: Here, infuriated — the opposite reaction to the repentant crowd in Acts 2:37.

chapters.n: Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, stands up and asks that the apostles be sent out briefly.

f.g: A leading rabbi, grandson of the famous Hillel, and teacher of Saul of Tarsus.
doctor = teacher.

chapters.n: He urges caution: be careful what you do to these men.

f.g: take heed = be careful.

chapters.n: He cites Theudas, who claimed to be someone important and gathered about four hundred men, but was killed, and his movement collapsed.

f.g: Little is known of this Theudas; scholars debate his identity and date.
came to nothing.

chapters.n: Then Judas the Galilean rose up during the census, led a revolt, and also perished, his followers scattered.

f.g: Led a tax revolt around AD 6, against the Roman census under Quirinius.
the census for taxation.

chapters.n: His advice: leave these men alone. If this movement is merely human, it will fail on its own.
But if it is from God, they cannot stop it — and might even find themselves fighting God. Wise counsel, and true.

f.w: if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it

f.g: haply = perhaps, by chance.

chapters.n: The council agrees, but still has the apostles flogged, orders them not to speak in Jesus’s name, and releases them.

f.g: Probably the synagogue punishment of up to 39 lashes.

chapters.n: The apostles leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for Jesus’s name.

f.w: rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name

chapters.n: Every day, in the temple and from house to house, they never stop teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.

f.w: they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ

chapters.n: As the Church grows, a complaint arises: Greek-speaking Jewish believers feel their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food compared with those of Aramaic-speaking believers. Growth brings new problems.

f.g: Hellenists — Jews raised outside the land of Israel whose main language was Greek.
Jews of the homeland who spoke Aramaic (and Hebrew).

chapters.n: The Twelve call the whole body of disciples together and explain that it wouldn’t be right for them to neglect preaching God’s word to manage food distribution.

f.g: It is not right or fitting.
Handle the daily food distribution (and perhaps its finances).

chapters.n: They ask the members to select seven men with good reputations, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to oversee this work. Even practical service requires spiritual qualifications.

f.w: full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom

chapters.n: The apostles will devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word — wise delegation lets each do what they are called to do.
The idea pleases everyone. They choose seven men, all with Greek names — likely from the very group that felt neglected. Stephen and Philip will become key figures in the chapters ahead.

f.w: Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost

f.g: Not the apostle Philip but “Philip the evangelist.”
A Gentile convert to Judaism from Antioch in Syria.

chapters.n: The congregation presents them to the apostles, who pray and lay their hands on them — setting them apart with authority for their calling.

f.w: they laid their hands on them
f.r: Numbers 27:18-23; Acts 13:3; Articles of Faith 1:5; D&C 42:11

chapters.n: God’s word keeps spreading, the number of disciples in Jerusalem grows rapidly, and even many priests accept the faith.

f.w: a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith
f.g: Probably ordinary priests serving in rotation at the temple, not the elite high-priestly families.

chapters.n: Stephen, full of grace and power, performs great wonders and signs among the people. His calling to serve tables didn’t limit his spiritual influence.
Opposition rises from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen — Jews from North Africa and Asia Minor — who debate with Stephen. Saul of Tarsus, from Cilicia, may well have been among them.

f.g: Libertines = Freedmen — descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, perhaps by Rome.
A region in southeastern Asia Minor whose chief city was Tarsus, Paul’s hometown.

chapters.n: They can’t stand against the wisdom and Spirit with which he speaks — just as Jesus had promised.

f.w: they were not able to resist the wisdom

chapters.n: So they secretly put men up to claiming they heard Stephen speak blasphemy against Moses and God — the same tactic used against Jesus.

f.g: suborned = secretly bribed or induced to give false testimony.

chapters.n: They stir up the people, elders, and scribes, seize Stephen, and drag him before the Sanhedrin.
They produce false witnesses who claim he never stops speaking against the temple and the law.

f.g: The temple.

chapters.n: The charge: Stephen said Jesus would destroy the temple and change the customs Moses gave — twisting Jesus’s actual teachings about the temple and the fulfillment of the law.

f.w: change the customs which Moses delivered us

chapters.n: Everyone in the council stares at Stephen and sees his face shining like an angel’s — like Moses coming down from the mount. Heaven is visibly with the accused.

The high priest asks Stephen whether the charges against him are true. What follows is the longest speech in Acts — a survey of Israel’s history showing that God was never confined to one place and that Israel often rejected his messengers.
Stephen addresses the council respectfully as brothers and fathers. He begins with Abraham: the glorious God appeared to him in Mesopotamia — outside the Holy Land, long before any temple.

f.w: The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham

f.g: Haran, a city in northern Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: God called Abraham to leave his land and relatives and go to a land God would show him.

f.w: Get thee out of thy country

chapters.n: Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans, settled in Haran, and after his father’s death God moved him into the land of Canaan where they now live.

f.g: The book of Abraham adds that his father Terah stayed in Haran and returned to idolatry.

chapters.n: God gave Abraham no land there — not even a foot’s length — yet promised it to him and his descendants, when he didn’t even have a child. Abraham lived by faith in promises.

f.w: not so much as to set his foot on
when as yet he had no child

chapters.n: God told Abraham his descendants would be foreigners in another land, enslaved and mistreated for about four hundred years.

f.g: entreat = treat; mistreat them.

chapters.n: God would judge the nation that enslaved them, and afterward they would come out and worship him in this place.
God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision. Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt — but God was with him. Stephen’s first example of Israel rejecting the one God chose to save them.
God rescued him from all his troubles, gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, and Pharaoh made him ruler over Egypt and the royal household.
A famine struck Egypt and Canaan, and their ancestors could find no food.

f.g: dearth = famine, scarcity.
Canaan.

chapters.n: Hearing there was grain in Egypt, Jacob sent his sons there the first time.

f.g: corn = grain, such as wheat or barley.

chapters.n: On their second visit Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned about Joseph’s family. Like Jesus, the rejected brother is recognized the second time.

f.w: at the second time Joseph was made known

chapters.n: Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives — seventy-five people in all.

f.g: 75 people. Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 gives 70, counting differently.

chapters.n: Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and the patriarchs died.

Their bodies were brought back to Shechem and buried in a tomb bought from the sons of Hamor. Stephen compresses several burial traditions; Genesis records Abraham buying a cave at Hebron and Jacob buying land at Shechem.

f.g: Shechem, in the region later called Samaria.

chapters.n: As the time approached for God to fulfill his promise to Abraham, the Israelites grew greatly in number in Egypt.

f.w: the people grew and multiplied in Egypt

chapters.n: Then a new king came to power who did not know about Joseph.

f.w: another king arose, which knew not Joseph

chapters.n: He schemed against their people and oppressed them, forcing them to abandon their infants so they would die.

f.g: subtilly = craftily, with cunning.

chapters.n: At that time Moses was born, a beautiful child in God’s sight, and was cared for at home for three months.

f.g: Literally “beautiful to God” — favored by God.

chapters.n: When he was set out, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and raised him as her own son.
Moses was educated in all the learning of Egypt and was powerful in words and deeds.

f.w: learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians
f.g: Egypt was renowned for learning in writing, mathematics, astronomy, and medicine.
Moses later felt slow of speech, but his words carried power.

chapters.n: At forty, he decided to visit his fellow Israelites.

f.g: Jewish tradition divided Moses’s 120 years into three periods of forty: Egypt, Midian, and the wilderness.

chapters.n: Seeing an Israelite being mistreated, he defended him and struck down the Egyptian.
Moses assumed his people would realize God was using him to deliver them — but they didn’t. Again, God’s chosen deliverer is misunderstood.
The next day he tried to make peace between two quarreling Israelites, reminding them they were brothers.

f.w: would have set them at one again
f.g: Tried to reconcile them, make them “at one” — the root idea of “atonement.”
strove = fought, quarreled.

chapters.n: But the man in the wrong pushed Moses away: “Who made you ruler and judge over us?”

f.w: Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?

chapters.n: “Are you going to kill me like you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”

f.g: diddest = did.

chapters.n: At this Moses fled and lived as a foreigner in Midian, where he had two sons.

f.g: Midian, a region east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

chapters.n: Forty years later, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the flames of a burning bush in the wilderness near Mount Sinai — once more, God revealing himself far from any temple.

f.w: a flame of fire in a bush

f.g: Sinai.

chapters.n: Amazed, Moses went closer to look, and the Lord’s voice spoke to him.
The Lord declared himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses trembled and didn’t dare look.

f.w: I am the God of thy fathers

chapters.n: The Lord told him to take off his sandals, because the place where he stood was holy ground. Holiness comes from God’s presence, even in a desert.

f.w: the place where thou standest is holy ground

chapters.n: God had seen his people’s suffering and heard their groaning, and had come down to rescue them; he would send Moses to Egypt.

f.w: I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people

chapters.n: Stephen drives the point home: the very Moses the people rejected — “Who made you ruler and judge?” — God sent as ruler and redeemer. The parallel to Jesus is unmistakable.

f.g: The Greek word for deliverer here is lytrōtēs — “redeemer,” a word that points to Christ.

chapters.n: Moses led them out, performing wonders in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This same Moses foretold that God would raise up a prophet like him from among them — the Messiah. Rejecting Jesus means rejecting Moses’s own words.

f.w: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you

chapters.n: Moses was with the congregation in the wilderness, with the angel at Sinai and with their ancestors, and received living words to pass on to them.

f.g: “Church” here means the assembly or congregation of Israel.
lively oracles = living words, revelations from God.

chapters.n: But their ancestors refused to obey him, pushed him aside, and in their hearts longed to go back to Egypt.

f.w: in their hearts turned back again into Egypt

chapters.n: They told Aaron to make them gods to lead them, since they didn’t know what had happened to Moses on the mountain.

f.w: Make us gods to go before us

f.g: wot = know.

chapters.n: They made a calf idol, sacrificed to it, and celebrated what their own hands had made — preferring a god they could build and control.

f.w: the works of their own hands

chapters.n: So God let them go their way, to worship the stars. Stephen quotes Amos: during forty years in the wilderness, were their sacrifices truly offered to God?

f.g: Sun, moon, and stars worshipped as gods.

f.w: as it is written in the book of the prophets

chapters.n: Instead they carried shrines of pagan gods like Moloch and the star-god Rephan, so God would exile them beyond Babylon.

f.g: A Canaanite god associated with child sacrifice.
The Greek Old Testament’s form of a star-god name (Hebrew Kiyyun), perhaps Saturn.
Amos says “beyond Damascus”; Stephen updates it to the Babylonian exile that actually happened.

chapters.n: Stephen turns to the sanctuary: their ancestors had the tabernacle of testimony in the wilderness, built exactly as God showed Moses. A portable sanctuary — God moved with his people.

f.g: fashion = pattern, design.

chapters.n: The next generation brought it into the land with Joshua when God drove out the nations, and it remained until David’s time.

f.g: Here “Jesus” is the Greek form of Joshua, Moses’s successor — not Jesus Christ.
drave = drove.

chapters.n: David found favor with God and asked to build a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.

f.w: desired to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob

chapters.n: But it was Solomon who built God a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in buildings made by human hands. Stephen isn’t against temples; he is against confining God to one.

f.w: the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands

chapters.n: He quotes Isaiah: heaven is God’s throne and earth his footstool — what house could anyone build for him?

f.w: Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool

chapters.n: “Didn’t my hand make all these things?”

f.w: Hath not my hand made all these things?

chapters.n: Then Stephen turns his history lesson into a direct indictment: they are stubborn and closed in heart and ears, always resisting the Holy Ghost, just like their ancestors.

f.g: Like an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

chapters.n: Which prophet did their fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One — and now they have betrayed and murdered him.

f.w: Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?

chapters.n: They received the law delivered by angels, yet failed to keep it — the very law they accuse Stephen of attacking.

f.g: disposition = arrangement, administration.

chapters.n: Enraged and cut to the heart, the council grinds their teeth at him.

f.w: gnashed on him with their teeth
f.g: gnash = grind the teeth in fury.

chapters.n: Full of the Holy Ghost, Stephen gazes into heaven and sees God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He sees two distinct beings — the Father and the Son.

f.w: saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God

chapters.n: He announces that the heavens are open and he sees the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. Elsewhere Jesus is pictured seated; here he stands — perhaps rising to receive or vindicate his faithful witness.

f.w: the Son of man standing on the right hand of God

chapters.n: They shout, cover their ears, and rush at him together.
They drag him out of the city and stone him. The witnesses lay their outer cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul — the future apostle Paul.

f.w: cast him out of the city

chapters.n: As the stones fall, Stephen prays, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” — echoing Jesus’s own words on the cross, now addressed to Jesus himself.
Kneeling, he cries out, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them,” and with that he dies — “falls asleep.” Like his Master, he forgives his killers. He is the first Christian martyr.

f.w: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge

chapters.n: Saul fully approved of Stephen’s killing. That day a severe persecution breaks out against the Jerusalem church, and believers scatter through Judea and Samaria — though the apostles stay. Persecution begins to fulfill Acts 1:8.

f.w: Saul was consenting unto his death
throughout the regions of Judæa and Samaria

chapters.n: Devout men bury Stephen and mourn deeply for him — openly grieving a man executed by the council took courage.

f.g: lamentation = loud mourning, wailing.

chapters.n: Saul tries to destroy the church, going house to house and dragging men and women off to prison.

f.g: Greek for ravaging, like a wild animal mauling prey.
haling = hauling, dragging.

chapters.n: But the scattered believers preach the word wherever they go. Scattering the seed only spreads it further.

f.w: went every where preaching the word

chapters.n: Philip — one of the Seven, not the apostle — goes to a city of Samaria and proclaims Christ there. Jews and Samaritans had been bitter rivals for centuries.

f.g: Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped at Mount Gerizim.

chapters.n: The crowds listen attentively to Philip as they hear his message and see his miracles.

f.g: united, all together.

chapters.n: Unclean spirits leave many people with loud shrieks, and many who are paralyzed or lame are healed.

f.g: palsy = paralysis.

chapters.n: The city is filled with joy. The gospel brings joy wherever it is received.
A man named Simon had long practiced magic there, amazing the Samaritans and claiming to be someone great.

f.g: Practiced magic arts. Later tradition calls him “Simon Magus.”
bewitched = amazed, astonished.

chapters.n: Everyone, from least to greatest, followed him, calling him “the Great Power of God.”

f.g: A title suggesting people saw him as divine or a divine emanation.

chapters.n: They followed him because his magic had impressed them for a long time.

f.g: for a long time.

chapters.n: But when they believe Philip’s message about God’s kingdom and Jesus Christ, men and women alike are baptized.

f.w: they were baptized, both men and women

chapters.n: Even Simon believes and is baptized. He follows Philip closely, astonished by the genuine miracles he sees.

f.g: His later behavior shows his conversion was incomplete.

chapters.n: When the apostles in Jerusalem hear that Samaria has accepted God’s word, they send Peter and John — the same John who once wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village.

f.w: they sent unto them Peter and John

chapters.n: When they arrive, they pray for the new converts to receive the Holy Ghost.

f.w: that they might receive the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Luke explains that the Holy Ghost hadn’t yet come on any of them; they had only been baptized in the Lord Jesus’s name. Baptism of water and of the Spirit are distinct ordinances.

f.w: only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus
f.g: Latter-day Saints have understood that Philip held authority to baptize but not to confer the Holy Ghost, which required the apostles’ higher authority.

chapters.n: Peter and John lay hands on them, and they receive the Holy Ghost — the ordinance Latter-day Saints call confirmation.

f.w: laid they their hands on them
f.r: Acts 19:5-6; Articles of Faith 1:4; D&C 33:15; Moroni 2:2

chapters.n: Seeing the Spirit given through the laying on of hands, Simon offers the apostles money.

f.g: The word “simony” — buying or selling church offices — comes from Simon’s name.

chapters.n: He asks them to sell him the power to give the Holy Ghost by laying on hands. He sees priesthood as a marketable skill.
Peter rebukes him sharply: “May your money perish with you,” for thinking God’s gift could be bought.

f.w: the gift of God may be purchased with money

chapters.n: Simon has no share in this ministry, because his heart isn’t right before God.

f.g: No share or portion at all.

f.w: thy heart is not right in the sight of God

chapters.n: Peter urges him to repent and pray, in hope that the intent of his heart might be forgiven. The door to repentance stays open.

f.w: Repent therefore of this thy wickedness

chapters.n: Peter perceives that Simon is full of bitter poison and bound by sin.

f.g: gall = a bitter, poisonous substance.

chapters.n: Simon asks them to pray for him that these warnings won’t befall him. Luke leaves his final fate unknown.

f.w: Pray ye to the Lord for me

chapters.n: Peter and John testify and preach, then head back to Jerusalem, preaching in many Samaritan villages along the way. The old wall between Jews and Samaritans is breaking down.

f.w: preached the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans

chapters.n: An angel tells Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. Leaving a thriving work for an empty road requires faith.

f.g: An ancient Philistine city near the Mediterranean coast, on the route to Egypt.
Either the road or old Gaza was deserted, a lonely route.

chapters.n: Philip goes, and meets an Ethiopian official — a eunuch in charge of the treasury of the Candace, queen of the Ethiopians — who had traveled to Jerusalem to worship.

f.g: Ancient Ethiopia (Kush) lay south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan.
A royal title (Kandake) of the queen mother of Kush, not a personal name.
Eunuchs were barred from full temple worship under the law, but Isaiah foresaw their welcome among God’s people.

chapters.n: Riding home in his chariot, he is reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah. Ancient people usually read aloud; a scroll of Isaiah would have been costly.

chapters.n: The Spirit tells Philip to go up and walk alongside the chariot.
Philip runs to it, hears the man reading Isaiah, and asks, “Do you understand what you’re reading?”
“How can I, unless someone guides me?” the official replies humbly, and invites Philip to sit with him.

f.w: except some man should guide me

chapters.n: He was reading Isaiah 53: like a sheep led to slaughter and a lamb silent before its shearer, he did not open his mouth.

f.w: He was led as a sheep to the slaughter

f.g: dumb = silent.

chapters.n: In his humiliation justice was denied him; who can speak of his descendants, for his life was taken from the earth?

f.g: Abinadi explains that Christ’s “seed” are those who follow the prophets and look to him for redemption.

chapters.n: The official asks: is the prophet speaking about himself or someone else? It’s exactly the right question.

f.w: of whom speaketh the prophet this?

chapters.n: Starting from that very passage, Philip tells him the good news about Jesus.

f.w: began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus

chapters.n: As they travel they come to water, and the official asks, “Look, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?”

f.w: what doth hinder me to be baptized?

chapters.n: Philip says he may if he believes with all his heart, and he confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. This verse is missing from many early manuscripts but reflects early baptismal practice.

f.w: If thou believest with all thine heart

chapters.n: He stops the chariot, both go down into the water, and Philip baptizes him — a description that fits baptism by immersion.

f.w: they went down both into the water

chapters.n: When they come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly takes Philip away. The official never sees him again but goes on his way rejoicing. Christian tradition credits him with helping bring the gospel to Africa.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip
he went on his way rejoicing

chapters.n: Philip turns up at Azotus and preaches in every town along the coast until he reaches Caesarea, where he later settles with his family.

f.g: The old Philistine city of Ashdod.
Caesarea Maritima, the Roman capital of Judea on the Mediterranean coast.

chapters.n: Saul is still breathing threats and murder against the Lord’s disciples. He goes to the high priest to extend his campaign. Luke paints him as the Church’s fiercest enemy — making what follows all the more remarkable.
He requests letters to the synagogues in Damascus authorizing him to arrest any followers of “the Way,” men or women, and bring them to Jerusalem in chains.

f.g: A major city in Syria, about 135 miles (220 km) north of Jerusalem, with a large Jewish community.
“The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

chapters.n: As he nears Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashes around him — brighter than the noonday sun, as Paul later recalls.
He falls to the ground and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” To persecute Christ’s disciples is to persecute Christ himself.

f.g: Doubling a name signals divine urgency and tenderness.

chapters.n: “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asks. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Saul learns the one he thought was dead is the living Lord. Jesus adds that Saul is only hurting himself by fighting against God.

f.w: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks
f.g: pricks = goads, pointed sticks used to drive oxen. An ox that kicks against the goad only wounds itself.

chapters.n: Trembling and stunned, Saul asks what the Lord wants him to do. He is told to go into the city, where he’ll be instructed. His question marks a total surrender.

f.w: Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?

chapters.n: His traveling companions stand speechless; they hear the sound but see no one. Paul’s later account says they saw the light but didn’t understand the voice — the JST of this verse reconciles the two.

f.w: hearing a voice, but seeing no man
f.g: The JST reads: “they saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they heard not the voice of him that spake to him.”

chapters.n: Saul gets up, but when he opens his eyes he can’t see. His companions lead him by the hand into Damascus — the hunter now helpless.

f.g: Physical blindness mirrors the spiritual blindness that is about to be healed.

chapters.n: For three days he is blind and neither eats nor drinks — a time of fasting, reflection, and repentance.
In Damascus lives a disciple named Ananias. The Lord calls him in a vision, and he answers, “Here I am, Lord.”

f.g: Paul later describes him as devout and respected by the Jews of Damascus. Not the Ananias of Acts 5.

chapters.n: The Lord tells him to go to Straight Street, to the house of Judas, and ask for Saul of Tarsus, who is praying.

f.w: the street which is called Straight
f.g: A main east–west street in Damascus that still exists today.
A prosperous city in Cilicia, known for learning.
The persecutor is now on his knees.

chapters.n: Saul has seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him to restore his sight. God prepares both people at once.
Ananias protests: he has heard from many people about the harm this man did to the saints in Jerusalem.

f.g: “Saints” — holy ones — is a common New Testament name for Church members.

chapters.n: And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest everyone who calls on Jesus’s name.

f.w: all that call on thy name

chapters.n: The Lord insists: go, for Saul is my chosen instrument to carry my name to Gentiles, kings, and the people of Israel.

f.g: vessel = instrument, tool.

chapters.n: The Lord will show him how much he must suffer for his name. Discipleship and sacrifice go together.

f.w: how great things he must suffer for my name's sake

chapters.n: Ananias goes, lays his hands on Saul, and calls him “Brother Saul.” He explains that Jesus sent him so Saul can see again and be filled with the Holy Ghost. Faith overcomes fear.

f.g: Ananias welcomes his former enemy as family.

chapters.n: Instantly something like scales falls from Saul’s eyes, and he can see. He gets up and is baptized.
After eating, he regains strength and spends some days with the disciples in Damascus — the very people he came to arrest.

f.g: meat = food.

chapters.n: Immediately he begins preaching in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

f.g: straightway = immediately.

f.w: that he is the Son of God

chapters.n: Everyone is astonished: isn’t this the man who devastated believers in Jerusalem and came here to arrest them?

f.w: Is not this he that destroyed them

chapters.n: Saul grows ever stronger and baffles the Jews of Damascus with proof that Jesus is the Messiah.

f.g: confounded = bewildered, unable to answer.
Literally “putting together” — comparing scriptures to show their fulfillment.

chapters.n: After many days, some Jewish leaders plot to kill him. Paul’s letters indicate this period included time in Arabia and lasted about three years.
Saul learns of the plot. They watch the city gates day and night to kill him.

f.g: laying await = lying in ambush.
Paul says the governor under King Aretas also guarded the city.

chapters.n: His disciples lower him at night through an opening in the wall in a large basket. The proud persecutor escapes in a humbling way.

f.w: let him down by the wall in a basket

chapters.n: In Jerusalem Saul tries to join the disciples, but they are afraid and don’t believe he’s truly a disciple. Trust takes time to rebuild.

f.g: assayed = attempted, tried.

f.w: they were all afraid of him

chapters.n: Barnabas — the “son of encouragement” — takes him to the apostles and vouches for him, telling how Saul saw the Lord and preached boldly in Damascus.
Saul moves freely among them in Jerusalem.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for living and working freely among people.

chapters.n: He speaks boldly in Jesus’s name and debates with the Greek-speaking Jews — the same group that opposed Stephen. Now they try to kill him too.

f.g: Hellenistic, Greek-speaking Jews.

chapters.n: When the believers learn of this, they take him down to Caesarea and send him home to Tarsus, where he will stay for some years.
The churches throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoy a time of peace. Strengthened, living in reverence for the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Ghost, they grow in number.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “the church” — one Church in many places.
edified = built up, strengthened.

f.w: the comfort of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Luke turns back to Peter, who travels among the congregations and visits the saints at Lydda.

f.g: A town about 25 miles northwest of Jerusalem, on the way to the coast (modern Lod).

chapters.n: There he finds a man named Aeneas, paralyzed and bedridden for eight years.

f.g: palsy = paralysis.

chapters.n: Peter tells him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.” He gets up at once. Peter makes clear the healer is Jesus.
Everyone in Lydda and the plain of Sharon sees him and turns to the Lord.

f.g: The plain of Sharon, the fertile coastal plain.

chapters.n: In the port city of Joppa lives a disciple named Tabitha (Greek, Dorcas — both mean “gazelle”). She is known for her constant good deeds and generosity to the poor.

f.g: Modern Jaffa, part of Tel Aviv — the port from which Jonah once fled.

f.w: full of good works and almsdeeds

chapters.n: She falls ill and dies. They wash her body and lay it in an upstairs room.

f.g: Washing the body was a customary preparation for burial.

chapters.n: Since Lydda is near Joppa, the disciples send two men to Peter, urging him to come without delay.

f.g: nigh = near; about 10–12 miles.

chapters.n: Peter goes with them. In the upper room widows stand around weeping, showing him the tunics and garments Dorcas had made for them. Her service is her best eulogy.

f.w: shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made

chapters.n: Peter sends everyone out, kneels and prays, then turns to the body and says, “Tabitha, arise.” She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up — much as Jesus did with Jairus’s daughter.

f.g: Very close to Jesus’s words “Talitha cumi” (“little girl, arise”) in Mark 5:41.

chapters.n: He gives her his hand, helps her up, and calls the saints and widows to present her alive.
News spreads through Joppa, and many believe in the Lord.

Peter stays many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. Tanners handled dead animals and were considered ritually unclean by strict Jews — a quiet sign that Peter’s boundaries are already loosening before chapter 10.

f.g: tarried = stayed.

chapters.n: In Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, lives Cornelius, a centurion in the Italian Cohort. This chapter marks a turning point: the gospel formally opens to the Gentiles.

f.g: Caesarea Maritima, Herod the Great’s port city and Rome’s administrative center in Judea.
A Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
band = cohort, a unit of several hundred soldiers, here apparently recruited from Italy.

chapters.n: Cornelius is devout: he and his household revere God, he gives generously to the poor, and he prays regularly. He is a “God-fearer” — a Gentile who worships Israel’s God without becoming a full convert.

f.g: A term for Gentiles who attended synagogue and honored the God of Israel.
alway = always, regularly.

chapters.n: About three in the afternoon — the hour of prayer — he clearly sees in a vision an angel of God come in and call his name.

f.g: evidently = clearly, distinctly.
About 3 p.m.

chapters.n: Frightened, Cornelius asks, “What is it, Lord?” The angel says his prayers and gifts have risen before God as a memorial — God has noticed and remembered them.

f.w: come up for a memorial before God
f.g: Like the smoke of an offering rising to heaven.

chapters.n: He is told to send men to Joppa for a man named Simon Peter. Even with an angel present, Cornelius must receive the gospel through God’s authorized servant.
Peter is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea, and will tell Cornelius what he must do.

f.w: he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do

f.g: lodgeth = is staying.

chapters.n: When the angel leaves, Cornelius calls two household servants and a devout soldier among his personal attendants.

f.g: Cornelius’s faith had influenced those around him.

chapters.n: He tells them everything and sends them to Joppa, about thirty miles south.

f.g: Roughly 30–35 miles (50 km), a journey of more than a day.

chapters.n: Around noon the next day, as the messengers near Joppa, Peter goes up onto the flat roof to pray.

f.g: Flat roofs were used as quiet places for rest and prayer.
About noon.

chapters.n: He becomes very hungry, and while the meal is being prepared, he falls into a trance. God prepares Peter’s heart at the same time he prepares Cornelius.

f.g: Greek ekstasis — a vision-state in which one’s mind is caught up by God.

chapters.n: He sees heaven open and something like a large sheet, held by its four corners, being lowered to the earth.

f.w: a great sheet knit at the four corners
f.g: Some see the four corners as representing the four directions — the whole world.

chapters.n: In it are all kinds of animals, reptiles, and birds — clean and unclean mixed together under the law of Moses.
A voice says, “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.”
Peter refuses: “No, Lord! I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” His words contain a contradiction — saying “no” to the Lord.

f.g: common = ritually impure, profane; forbidden under the dietary laws.

chapters.n: The voice replies, “What God has made clean, you must not call common.” The lesson is about food — and, as Peter will learn, about people.

f.w: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common

chapters.n: This happens three times, and the sheet is taken back up into heaven. Peter, who denied Jesus three times and was asked three times “Lovest thou me?”, now learns another lesson in threes.

f.g: thrice = three times.

chapters.n: While Peter is puzzling over the vision, the men from Cornelius find the house and stand at the gate. God’s timing is precise.

f.g: doubted = was perplexed, unsure of the meaning.

chapters.n: They call out, asking if Simon called Peter is staying there.

f.g: was staying there as a guest.

chapters.n: As Peter keeps thinking about the vision, the Spirit tells him three men are looking for him.
The Spirit says to go down and go with them without hesitation, because the Spirit himself sent them.

f.g: Or “without discriminating” — making no distinction between Jew and Gentile.

chapters.n: Peter goes down, identifies himself, and asks why they’ve come.

f.w: I am he whom ye seek
f.g: Peter meets them openly rather than hiding behind the gate.

chapters.n: They describe Cornelius as a righteous, God-fearing man respected by the whole Jewish nation, who was directed by a holy angel to invite Peter to his house and hear his message.

f.g: just = righteous, upright.
of good reputation.

chapters.n: Peter invites these Gentiles in as his guests — itself a step across a cultural line. The next day he leaves with them, along with some believers from Joppa as witnesses.

f.w: called he them in, and lodged them
f.g: Hosting Gentiles was something many devout Jews avoided.
Six Jewish believers went along, giving multiple witnesses.

chapters.n: The day after, they arrive in Caesarea. Cornelius is waiting and has gathered his relatives and close friends — he wants others to hear too.

f.w: had called together his kinsmen and near friends

chapters.n: As Peter enters, Cornelius falls at his feet in reverence.

f.g: Bowed down in deep reverence — a gesture Peter will not accept.

chapters.n: Peter lifts him up: “Stand up; I am only a man myself.” God’s servants point worship to God alone.

f.w: I myself also am a man

chapters.n: Talking with Cornelius, Peter goes inside and finds a large gathering.

f.w: found many that were come together
f.g: A house full of Gentiles eager to hear.

chapters.n: Peter acknowledges that Jewish custom forbids close association with Gentiles, but God has shown him not to call any person common or unclean. He has understood the vision: it was about people, not just food.

f.w: an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company
f.g: Not written in the law of Moses itself, but a strong tradition about ritual purity.

f.w: I should not call any man common or unclean

chapters.n: So he came without objection when invited, and now asks why they sent for him.

f.g: gainsay = object, speak against.

chapters.n: Cornelius explains that four days earlier, while fasting and praying at three in the afternoon, a man in shining clothes stood before him.

f.w: a man stood before me in bright clothing

chapters.n: The messenger said his prayer had been heard and his gifts to the poor remembered by God.
He was told to send for Peter at Simon the tanner’s house by the sea, who would speak to him.

f.w: who, when he cometh, shall speak unto thee

chapters.n: He sent at once and thanks Peter for coming. Now they are all present before God, ready to hear whatever the Lord has commanded. A model of how to receive a message from God.

f.w: we all here present before God

chapters.n: Peter begins: “Now I truly understand that God shows no favoritism.” This is one of the great breakthroughs of the New Testament.

f.w: God is no respecter of persons
f.g: God does not show partiality based on nationality or status.

chapters.n: In every nation, anyone who reveres God and does what is right is acceptable to him.
Peter summarizes the message God sent to Israel: the good news of peace through Jesus Christ — who is Lord of all, Jews and Gentiles alike.
They already know the story, which spread throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee after John’s baptism.

f.g: published = proclaimed, made known.

f.w: after the baptism which John preached

chapters.n: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and power. He went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him. A beautiful one-sentence summary of Christ’s ministry.

f.w: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power

chapters.n: The apostles are witnesses of everything he did in the Jewish countryside and in Jerusalem — where they killed him by hanging him on a tree.
God raised him up on the third day and let him be seen.
Not by everyone, but by witnesses God had chosen beforehand — the apostles, who ate and drank with him after he rose. Eating with him proved his resurrected body was real.

f.w: did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead

chapters.n: He commanded them to preach and testify that he is the one God appointed to judge the living and the dead.

f.w: the Judge of quick and dead
f.g: quick = living.

chapters.n: All the prophets testify of him: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

f.w: To him give all the prophets witness

chapters.n: While Peter is still speaking, the Holy Ghost falls on all who are listening. God interrupts the sermon to settle the question. Latter-day Saints distinguish this powerful witness of the Spirit, which can come before baptism, from the gift of the Holy Ghost conferred afterward.

f.w: the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word

chapters.n: The Jewish believers who came with Peter are astonished that the Holy Ghost has been poured out even on Gentiles.

f.g: Jewish Christians.

chapters.n: They hear the Gentiles speaking in tongues and praising God — a “Gentile Pentecost.” Peter then speaks up.

f.g: magnify = praise, exalt.

chapters.n: Peter asks: can anyone refuse water to baptize these people, who have received the Holy Ghost just as we did?
He orders them baptized in the name of the Lord. They ask him to stay for some days — and Peter, once unwilling to eat with Gentiles, now lives among them.

f.w: he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord

f.g: tarry = stay. Peter would later be criticized in Jerusalem for eating with Gentiles.

chapters.n: News spread quickly: Gentiles — non-Jews — had accepted the gospel at Cornelius’s house. For a church that was entirely Jewish so far, this was startling and needed explaining.

f.w: the Gentiles had also received the word of God

chapters.n: Back in Jerusalem, some Jewish believers who insisted on the law of Moses challenged Peter. “They of the circumcision” means Jewish Christians who felt Gentile converts must first become Jews.

f.w: they that were of the circumcision
f.g: Jewish Christians who held that circumcision and the law of Moses were still required.

chapters.n: Their complaint was not mainly about baptism but about table fellowship. Strict Jews avoided eating with Gentiles, whose food and homes were considered ritually unclean.
Instead of arguing, Peter simply told the story step by step. Letting the facts speak was the wisest way to show that God, not Peter, had opened this door.

f.g: Recounted, told over again.
In sequence, from start to finish.

chapters.n: Peter retells his vision in Joppa, the seaport where he had been staying. A great sheet came down from heaven, lowered by its four corners.

f.g: Modern Jaffa, the port next to today’s Tel Aviv.

f.w: in a trance I saw a vision

chapters.n: The sheet held every kind of animal, including ones the law of Moses forbade Israelites to eat. Peter looked closely, and the sight would have shocked any faithful Jew.
A voice commanded Peter to kill and eat. The command seemed to contradict everything he had kept his whole life.
Peter protested that he had never eaten anything forbidden. “Common” here means ordinary or profane — not set apart as clean under the law.

f.g: “Common” = ritually ordinary, unfit for a holy people; “unclean” = forbidden by the law.

chapters.n: The heart of the vision: what God has made clean, Peter must not call unclean. The lesson went beyond food — it was about people, as Peter came to understand.

f.w: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common

chapters.n: The vision repeated three times, underlining its importance. Then everything was taken back up to heaven.
Right at that moment, messengers from Cornelius arrived. The timing showed Peter that the vision and the visitors belonged together.

f.g: Roman capital of Judea on the Mediterranean coast, about 30 miles north of Joppa.

chapters.n: The Spirit told Peter to go without hesitating. He wisely brought six Jewish brethren as witnesses — and they are now present in Jerusalem to confirm his account.

f.g: Without hesitation or making distinctions.

chapters.n: Cornelius had also been visited by an angel, who told him to send for Peter. God had been preparing both men at the same time.

f.w: he had seen an angel in his house

chapters.n: The angel promised that Peter’s message would bring salvation to Cornelius and his whole household. The gospel was meant for families.

f.w: thou and all thy house shall be saved

chapters.n: Before Peter had even finished, the Holy Ghost came upon these Gentiles just as it had on the apostles at Pentecost. God himself had given the sign of acceptance.

f.w: as on us at the beginning

chapters.n: Peter remembered Jesus’ promise that his disciples would be baptized with the Holy Ghost. Seeing it happen to Gentiles proved they were included.

f.w: ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Peter’s conclusion: if God gave them the same gift he gave us, who was I to stand in God’s way? Refusing them baptism would have meant resisting God.

f.w: what was I, that I could withstand God?

chapters.n: The critics were satisfied and praised God. A major turning point: the Church now officially recognized that repentance and eternal life were open to the Gentiles too.

f.g: Repentance that leads to eternal life.

chapters.n: Luke now picks up another thread. Believers who fled Jerusalem after Stephen’s death carried the gospel north — but at first only to fellow Jews.

f.w: the persecution that arose about Stephen

f.g: Phoenicia — the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, in modern Lebanon.

chapters.n: Some Jewish believers from Cyprus and North Africa took a bold step in Antioch: they taught Greek-speaking Gentiles too. “Grecians” here likely means Greeks rather than Greek-speaking Jews.

f.g: Antioch in Syria, the third-largest city of the Roman Empire.
A city in North Africa, in modern Libya.

chapters.n: God blessed their work, and many people turned to the Lord. Antioch would become the home base for the Church’s mission to the Gentiles.

f.g: A biblical idiom for God’s power and help.

chapters.n: The Jerusalem leaders sent Barnabas to check on this new growth. He was a trusted, generous disciple and himself from Cyprus.
Barnabas didn’t come to criticize — he saw God’s grace at work and rejoiced. He urged the new converts to hold to the Lord with full determination.

f.g: With firm, deliberate commitment.

chapters.n: Luke praises Barnabas as a good man, full of the Spirit and faith. Under such leadership, still more people joined the Church.
Barnabas went to Tarsus, Paul’s hometown, to look for Saul. He remembered this converted persecutor and saw the work he could do.
Barnabas and Saul taught in Antioch for a full year. There the followers of Jesus were first called “Christians” — people belonging to Christ.

f.g: Greek Christianoi — “partisans of Christ”; probably a nickname given by outsiders.

chapters.n: Prophets — inspired teachers who could foretell events — came from Jerusalem. The gift of prophecy was active in the early Church.
Agabus foretold a severe famine across the Roman world. It happened under Emperor Claudius (AD 41–54), when historians record several food shortages.

f.g: Famine, scarcity of food.

chapters.n: The Antioch saints each gave what they could to help the believers in Judea. A Gentile-founded church caring for Jewish saints showed their unity in Christ.

f.w: every man according to his ability

chapters.n: They sent the relief to the Jerusalem elders through Barnabas and Saul. This is the first mention of elders as leaders in the Church.

f.g: Local leaders of the Church; an office of the priesthood.

chapters.n: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea from AD 41 to 44. He began to persecute Church leaders to win favor with the people.

f.g: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and nephew of Herod Antipas.
Harm, mistreat.

chapters.n: James, son of Zebedee and one of the original Twelve, became the first apostle to die as a martyr. Jesus had foretold that James would share his “cup” of suffering.
