Seeing that the execution was popular, Herod arrested Peter too. It was Passover season, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims — an echo of Jesus’ own arrest.
Herod placed Peter under heavy guard — sixteen soldiers in shifts — planning a public trial after the feast. “Easter” here translates the Greek word for Passover.

f.g: Four squads of four soldiers each, rotating through the night watches.
Greek pascha — Passover. Most modern translations read “Passover.”

chapters.n: Peter was locked away, but the Church prayed earnestly and constantly for him. Luke sets the contrast clearly: Herod’s power on one side, the saints’ prayers on the other.

f.g: Earnestly, intensely — the Greek suggests stretched-out, fervent prayer.

chapters.n: On the night before his trial, Peter was asleep — chained to two soldiers, with more guards at the door. His calm sleep shows remarkable trust in the Lord.
An angel appeared, light filled the cell, and he nudged Peter awake. The chains simply fell off — no human help was involved.
The angel gave simple, practical instructions: get dressed, put on your sandals, wrap your cloak around you, and follow. Heavenly help often comes with ordinary steps for us to take.

f.g: Tie up your tunic with your belt, ready to move.

chapters.n: Peter followed, but it all felt so unreal that he thought he was seeing a vision. “Wist not” means he did not realize it was actually happening.

f.g: Wist = knew; he did not know.

chapters.n: They passed two guard posts and reached the iron gate to the city, which opened by itself. After one street, the angel vanished.

f.g: Guard post or watch station.
By itself — without anyone opening it.

chapters.n: Standing in the street, Peter came to his senses. Now he knew for certain the Lord had rescued him from Herod and from what the crowds were hoping to see.

f.w: Now I know of a surety

chapters.n: Peter went to the home of Mary, mother of John Mark, where believers were praying for him. Her house seems to have been a gathering place for the Jerusalem church.

f.g: Traditionally the author of the Gospel of Mark; cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10).

chapters.n: A servant girl named Rhoda came to answer his knock at the outer gate. Luke preserves her name, a small personal touch in the story.

f.g: Young woman; here likely a household servant.
A Greek name meaning “rose.”

chapters.n: Rhoda recognized Peter’s voice and was so excited that she ran to tell everyone — leaving him standing outside. It’s a delightfully human moment.
Those praying for Peter’s release couldn’t believe it when it came! They called Rhoda crazy, then guessed it must be his “angel” — a guardian spirit, as some Jews then believed.

f.g: You’re out of your mind.
Some Jews of the time believed each person had a guardian angel who could resemble them.

chapters.n: Peter kept knocking until they finally opened the door. They were amazed to see him standing there.
Peter quieted them, told the story, and asked them to tell James and the others. This James is the Lord’s brother, now a leader in Jerusalem. Peter then went into hiding.
At dawn the soldiers were in a panic. Losing a prisoner was a serious matter for Roman-style guards.

f.g: A big commotion — Luke’s understated way of saying something major.

chapters.n: Herod searched without success and had the guards executed, as the law of the time often required for guards who lost a prisoner. Then he left for Caesarea.

f.g: The Roman administrative capital on the coast.

chapters.n: Herod was angry with the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. They depended on his territory for food, so they won over his chamberlain Blastus and asked for peace.

f.g: Phoenician port cities north of Galilee, in modern Lebanon.
Personal attendant to the king, an influential court official.

chapters.n: On an appointed day, Herod appeared in his royal robes and gave a public speech. The Jewish historian Josephus describes a robe of silver that shone in the sun.

f.g: Josephus (Antiquities 19.8.2) also records this event and Herod’s sudden death.

chapters.n: The crowd flattered him, shouting that he spoke like a god. Herod accepted the praise instead of rejecting it.
Because he took glory that belonged to God, an angel struck him, and he died a painful death. The persecutor who killed James met a swift end.

f.w: he gave not God the glory

f.g: Died; breathed his last.

chapters.n: A short but powerful summary: tyrants rise and fall, but the word of God keeps spreading. Herod is gone, and the Church grows.

f.w: the word of God grew and multiplied

chapters.n: Barnabas and Saul finished delivering the famine relief and returned to Antioch, bringing John Mark with them. This sets the stage for their first missionary journey.
The Antioch church had a diverse group of leaders: Barnabas from Cyprus, Simeon “the Black,” Lucius from North Africa, Manaen who grew up in Herod Antipas’s court, and Saul from Tarsus.

f.g: Latin for “black” — perhaps describing Simeon’s dark complexion; possibly African.
Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who beheaded John the Baptist.

chapters.n: While these leaders worshipped and fasted, the Holy Ghost called Barnabas and Saul to a special mission. The call came by revelation, not by personal ambition.

f.g: Served, worshipped.

chapters.n: After more fasting and prayer, the leaders laid their hands on them and sent them out. This setting apart by the laying on of hands is still how callings are given in the Church.
So begins Paul’s first missionary journey (about AD 47–48). They went down to the port of Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island.

f.g: The seaport serving Antioch, about 16 miles west.

chapters.n: At Salamis, on Cyprus’s east coast, they began by teaching in the Jewish synagogues — Paul’s usual pattern. John Mark came along as their assistant.

f.g: Here, an assistant or helper.

chapters.n: Crossing the island to Paphos, the Roman capital on the west coast, they met a Jewish magician and false prophet named Bar-jesus.

f.g: Aramaic “son of Joshua/Jesus” — an ironic name for an enemy of Christ.
Greek magos — a magician or occult practitioner.

chapters.n: Bar-jesus served as an adviser to the Roman governor, Sergius Paulus. The governor was thoughtful and intelligent, and he sent for the missionaries to hear their message.

f.g: Proconsul — Roman governor of a senatorial province.
Intelligent, wise, discerning.

chapters.n: The magician, also called Elymas, worked against the missionaries and tried to keep the governor from believing. He likely feared losing his influence.
From here on Luke uses Paul, Saul’s Roman name, which fits his mission among Gentiles. Filled with the Spirit, Paul fixed his eyes on Elymas.

f.g: Latin Paulus, meaning “small.” Paul likely had both names from birth, as a Jew and a Roman citizen.

chapters.n: Paul sharply rebuked Elymas as a deceiver and enemy of righteousness, twisting the Lord’s straight paths. The strong words expose spiritual opposition for what it is.

f.g: Deceit, craftiness.

f.w: pervert the right ways of the Lord

chapters.n: Elymas was struck with temporary blindness — the man who blinded others spiritually now groped for someone to lead him. Paul himself once had been led by the hand when blinded.

f.g: For a time — the blindness was temporary, leaving room for repentance.

f.w: seeking some to lead him by the hand

chapters.n: The governor believed, amazed not just by the miracle but by the teaching about the Lord. He became one of the first high-ranking Roman converts.

f.w: astonished at the doctrine of the Lord

chapters.n: Paul now leads the group. They sailed to Perga on the south coast of modern Turkey, where John Mark left and went home — a decision that later caused a rift between Paul and Barnabas.

f.g: A coastal region of southern Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

chapters.n: They traveled inland to another Antioch, in the region of Pisidia. On the Sabbath they went to the synagogue and sat with the congregation.

f.g: A Roman colony in central Asia Minor — different from Antioch in Syria.

chapters.n: After readings from the law and the prophets, synagogue leaders often invited visiting teachers to speak. Paul took the opening.

f.g: The scripture readings of a synagogue service: the five books of Moses and a passage from the prophets.
Officials who arranged the service.

chapters.n: Paul addressed two groups: Jews (“men of Israel”) and God-fearing Gentiles who worshipped with them. This is Paul’s first recorded sermon.

f.g: Gentiles who believed in Israel’s God and attended synagogue without fully converting.

chapters.n: Paul begins with Israel’s story: God chose their ancestors, made them a great people in Egypt, and led them out with power.

f.g: A Hebrew image of mighty, visible power.

f.w: brought he them out of it

chapters.n: For forty years God patiently put up with Israel’s behavior in the wilderness. Some ancient manuscripts read “cared for them” instead of “suffered their manners.”

f.g: Bore with their ways; some manuscripts read “carried them as a nurse.”

chapters.n: God drove out the seven nations of Canaan and gave Israel the land as an inheritance, divided among the tribes by lot.

f.g: Canaan, in Greek spelling.

chapters.n: Then came the era of the judges until Samuel. The 450 years likely counts the whole period from Egypt to the conquest, as many scholars read the Greek.
Israel asked for a king, and God gave them Saul of the tribe of Benjamin — the same tribe as Paul, whose Hebrew name was also Saul.

f.g: Kish, Saul’s father, in Greek spelling.

chapters.n: God replaced Saul with David, whom he described as “a man after mine own heart” — someone devoted to doing God’s will.

f.w: a man after mine own heart

chapters.n: Here is Paul’s main point: God kept his promise by raising up a Savior, Jesus, from David’s family line.
Before Jesus began his ministry, John the Baptist called all Israel to repent and be baptized, preparing them for the Messiah.
As John’s mission neared its end, he made clear he was not the Messiah. Someone greater was coming, so great that John felt unworthy even to untie his sandals.

f.w: whose shoes of his feet I am not worthy to loose

chapters.n: Paul speaks directly to his hearers: this message of salvation is meant for you — both Abraham’s descendants and Gentiles who worship God.

f.w: children of the stock of Abraham

chapters.n: The people of Jerusalem and their leaders didn’t recognize Jesus or understand the prophets they read every week — yet in condemning him they fulfilled those very prophecies.

f.w: they have fulfilled them in condemning him

chapters.n: Even though they could find no crime deserving death, they pressed Pilate to have Jesus executed.

f.w: they found no cause of death in him

chapters.n: Everything prophesied about him came true. They took his body down from the cross — “the tree” — and buried it in a tomb.

f.g: The cross; an allusion to Deuteronomy 21:22-23.

chapters.n: Four short words carry the whole gospel: “But God raised him.” Death was not the end of Jesus’ story.

f.w: God raised him from the dead

chapters.n: The risen Lord appeared over many days to the disciples who had followed him from Galilee. They are living witnesses of his resurrection.
Paul and Barnabas bring good news: the promise God made to the ancestors of Israel has come true.

f.g: Good news — the meaning of “gospel.”

f.g: A town about 60 miles southeast of Lystra.

chapters.n: After making many disciples in Derbe, they bravely retraced their route through the very cities that had persecuted them.

f.g: Strengthening, establishing.

chapters.n: They ordained elders to lead each branch and, with prayer and fasting, entrusted them to the Lord. The Church was organized with local priesthood leadership.

f.g: Greek cheirotoneō — appointed, literally “stretched out the hand.”

chapters.n: They passed back through the Pisidia region and came down to the coastal area of Pamphylia.
They preached in Perga, which they had skipped earlier, and then went to the port of Attalia.

f.g: Modern Antalya, a port on Turkey’s southern coast.

chapters.n: From there they sailed back to Antioch in Syria, where their mission had begun. Their assignment was complete.

f.w: recommended to the grace of God

chapters.n: They gathered the church and reported everything God had done — especially how he opened “the door of faith” to the Gentiles.
Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch a long while with the believers, resting and teaching before the next challenge arose.
A serious dispute arose. Teachers from Judea insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved — in effect, become Jews first.

f.w: Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses

chapters.n: Paul and Barnabas argued strongly against this. The Antioch church sent them to Jerusalem so the apostles and elders could settle the question — the Church’s proper way to resolve doctrine.

f.w: unto the apostles and elders about this question

chapters.n: On the way they told congregations in Phoenicia and Samaria about the Gentile conversions, and everyone rejoiced.

f.g: Phoenicia, the coastal region of modern Lebanon.

chapters.n: The Jerusalem church and its leaders welcomed them warmly, and they reported all that God had done through them.

f.w: the sect of the Pharisees which believed
f.g: Jewish Christians who came from the strict Pharisee party.

chapters.n: The apostles and elders met in council to consider the matter carefully. This gathering is often called the Jerusalem Council (about AD 49).

God, who sees the heart, showed his approval of the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Ghost just as he had to the Jewish believers.
God made no distinction between Jew and Gentile, cleansing their hearts through faith — not through circumcision.
Why test God by placing a burden on converts that even we Jews could never fully carry? Peter calls the ritual law a heavy yoke.

f.g: Test God — challenge what he has already made clear.

chapters.n: Peter’s great conclusion: both Jews and Gentiles are saved the same way — through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.

f.w: through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved

chapters.n: The assembly fell silent and listened as Barnabas and Paul described the miracles God had worked among the Gentiles — more evidence of God’s approval.

f.g: A Hebrew form of Simon — Peter’s original name.

chapters.n: James shows that this agrees with the prophets. Scripture and revelation confirm each other.

f.w: build again the tabernacle of David

chapters.n: The purpose: that all people — including Gentiles who take God’s name upon them — might seek the Lord. The restoration of Israel would bless the whole world.

chapters.n: God has known his plans from the very beginning. Including the Gentiles was no afterthought.

chapters.n: Moses’ law is read every Sabbath in synagogues everywhere, so these basic courtesies would help Gentile and Jewish believers live and eat together in peace.

chapters.n: Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, gave many words of encouragement and strengthened the church.

chapters.n: The believers in Lystra and Iconium spoke highly of Timothy. His good reputation prepared him for a calling.

f.w: circumcised him because of the Jews

chapters.n: As they traveled, they shared the Jerusalem council’s decisions with each branch so they could follow them.

Fortune-telling.

f.g: Fair-minded, generous in spirit.

Greek spermologos — “seed-picker,” someone who picks up scraps of ideas.

chapters.n: God doesn’t need anything from us — he gives life, breath, and everything else. We depend on him, not he on us.

The Lord promised protection and said, “I have much people in this city” — many prepared hearts not yet found.

f.w: I have much people in this city

chapters.n: Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth, teaching God’s word — one of his longest stays anywhere.
When Gallio became governor of Achaia (about AD 51), opponents brought Paul to court. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s term, helping scholars date Paul’s travels.

f.g: Brother of the philosopher Seneca; proconsul of Achaia about AD 51–52.
Greek bēma — the raised platform where officials heard cases.

chapters.n: They accused Paul of teaching worship that violated the law — hoping Rome would treat Christianity as an illegal religion.
Before Paul could defend himself, Gallio cut in: if this were a real crime, I would hear it.

f.g: Here, villainy or serious wrongdoing.

chapters.n: But since this was a dispute about words, names, and Jewish law, Gallio refused to judge it. His ruling effectively let Christianity be treated as part of Judaism, a legal religion.
He dismissed them from his court.

f.g: Drove.

chapters.n: The crowd then beat Sosthenes, the new synagogue leader, in front of the court, and Gallio ignored it. A Sosthenes later appears as Paul’s fellow believer — possibly the same man.
After more time, Paul sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchrea, Corinth’s eastern port, he cut his hair to complete a vow — probably a Nazarite-style vow of devotion.

f.g: Corinth’s harbor on the Aegean side.

chapters.n: They reached Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila stayed. Paul reasoned briefly with the Jews in the synagogue.

f.g: Major city of the province of Asia, home of the great temple of Artemis (Diana).

chapters.n: The Ephesian Jews asked him to stay longer, but he declined.
He wanted to reach Jerusalem for an upcoming feast but promised to return “if God will” — a humble way to make plans.
He landed at Caesarea, went up to greet the church in Jerusalem, then returned to Antioch — ending his second missionary journey.

f.g: Gone up to Jerusalem, which sits high in the hills.

chapters.n: After a stay in Antioch, Paul set out again through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening the disciples. This begins his third missionary journey.
Meanwhile Apollos came to Ephesus — a Jew from Alexandria in Egypt, a gifted speaker deeply versed in the scriptures.

f.g: Great Egyptian city and center of Jewish learning in Greek.

chapters.n: Apollos taught about Jesus with zeal and accuracy, but he knew only John’s baptism. His knowledge was sincere but incomplete.
Priscilla and Aquila heard him, took him aside privately, and explained God’s way more completely. A model of kind, discreet correction — and a woman taking part in teaching.

f.w: expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly
f.g: Explained more accurately and fully.

chapters.n: When Apollos decided to go to Greece, the Ephesian believers wrote a letter of recommendation. In Corinth he greatly helped the believers.

f.g: Southern Greece, including Corinth.

chapters.n: He powerfully refuted his opponents in public debate, proving from scripture that Jesus is the Christ.

f.w: shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ

chapters.n: Paul traveled through the inland highlands and reached Ephesus, where he met some disciples — likely followers of John the Baptist’s teaching.

f.g: The interior highland regions of Asia Minor.

chapters.n: Paul asked whether they had received the Holy Ghost. They hadn’t even heard of it — a sign their instruction and baptism were incomplete.

f.w: Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?

chapters.n: Paul asked about their baptism. They had received John’s baptism — perhaps from someone without authority, or without understanding of Christ.
Paul explained that John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance pointing forward to Jesus. John always testified of the One coming after him.
They were then baptized in Jesus’ name. Latter-day Saints see this as an example that baptism must be done with proper authority and understanding.

f.w: they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus

chapters.n: Paul laid his hands on them and they received the Holy Ghost, speaking in tongues and prophesying. Baptism is followed by the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands.
About twelve men were part of this group.
For three months Paul taught boldly in the synagogue about the kingdom of God.
When some hardened and publicly mocked “the Way,” Paul moved the disciples to the lecture hall of Tyrannus and taught there daily.

f.g: “The Way” — an early name for the Christian movement.
Some, several.
Lecture hall.

chapters.n: For two years the message spread from Ephesus across the whole province of Asia — probably when churches like Colossae and Laodicea were founded.

f.w: all they which dwelt in Asia heard

chapters.n: God worked unusual miracles through Paul.

f.g: Extraordinary, not ordinary.

chapters.n: Even cloths that had touched Paul — like the sweat rags and work aprons of a tentmaker — were taken to the sick, who were healed. The power came from God, not the cloth.

f.g: Sweat-cloths and work aprons, probably from Paul’s trade.

chapters.n: Some traveling Jewish exorcists tried using Jesus’ name like a magic spell, without faith or authority.

f.g: Wandering, traveling from place to place.
Command by oath, solemnly charge.

chapters.n: Seven sons of Sceva, who claimed priestly status, were doing this.

f.g: Possibly a self-claimed title; no Sceva is known among Jerusalem’s high priests.

chapters.n: The evil spirit replied: I know Jesus and I know Paul — but who are you? Using holy names without true authority has no power.

f.w: Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?

chapters.n: The possessed man attacked all seven and overpowered them. They fled the house bruised and stripped of their clothes.
Word spread through Ephesus, and people were filled with awe. The name of Jesus was honored, not misused.

f.g: Honored, praised.

chapters.n: Many believers came forward and openly confessed their past practices.

f.g: Disclosed their practices — likely their magic spells.

chapters.n: Converts who had practiced magic burned their scrolls publicly, worth fifty thousand silver coins — roughly a laborer’s wage for fifty thousand days. True repentance can cost something real.

f.g: Magic, sorcery. Ephesus was famous for its magical scrolls.
Likely drachmas; one drachma was about a day’s wage.

chapters.n: The word of the Lord grew powerfully and prevailed.
Paul, guided by the Spirit, planned to revisit Greece, go to Jerusalem, and then see Rome. This sets the direction for the rest of Acts.
He sent Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia while he stayed in Asia a little longer.
Around that time a major disturbance broke out over “the Way.”

f.g: A big commotion.

chapters.n: Demetrius, a silversmith, made small silver shrines of the goddess Diana (Artemis), a profitable business for local craftsmen.

f.g: Greek Artemis. Her temple in Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
Souvenir models of the temple or goddess sold to pilgrims.

chapters.n: He gathered the craftsmen and reminded them that their wealth depended on this trade.
Paul’s teaching that handmade gods aren’t gods at all was persuading crowds across Asia, and it was hurting sales.

f.w: they be no gods, which are made with hands

chapters.n: Demetrius warned that their trade would collapse and that the great goddess’s temple and reputation would suffer. Money and civic pride were tangled together.

f.g: Brought into disrepute, made worthless.

chapters.n: The craftsmen became furious and started chanting, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!”
The city erupted. The mob seized two of Paul’s Macedonian companions, Gaius and Aristarchus, and rushed into the great theatre, which held about 25,000 people.

f.g: The huge open-air theatre of Ephesus, whose ruins still stand.

chapters.n: Paul wanted to go in and address the crowd, but the disciples wouldn’t let him.
Even some high officials of the province, friends of Paul, sent word urging him not to risk entering the theatre.

f.g: Asiarchs — prominent leaders of the province, often wealthy patrons of civic festivals.
Risk himself.

chapters.n: The crowd was in chaos, shouting different things — most didn’t even know why they were there. Luke shows how mobs work.
The Jewish community pushed forward a man named Alexander, probably to distance themselves from the Christians. He motioned to speak.
But when they saw he was a Jew — who also rejected idols — the crowd drowned him out, chanting for two hours, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!”
Finally the city clerk calmed them. Everyone knows Ephesus guards Diana’s temple and the sacred image “fallen from heaven,” he said — likely a meteorite revered as her image.

f.g: The chief civic official of Ephesus, who handled public assemblies.

f.w: the image which fell down from Jupiter
f.g: A sacred object believed to have fallen from the sky — perhaps a meteorite.

chapters.n: Since no one can deny that, he argued, there’s no need to riot. Stay calm and don’t act rashly.
These men haven’t robbed temples or insulted your goddess. The clerk effectively declared Paul’s companions innocent.

f.g: Temple robbers.

chapters.n: If Demetrius has a complaint, the courts are open and the governors are available. Let them press charges legally.

f.g: Proconsuls — Roman governors.
Bring charges, sue.

chapters.n: Any other matters should be settled in a lawful, regularly called city assembly — not a mob.
The clerk warned that Rome might punish the city for this unlawful riot. Rome watched closely for civil disorder.

f.g: Disorderly gathering, riot.

chapters.n: With that, he dismissed the crowd. Once again, a Roman official found no legal fault with the Christians.
Once the riot was over, Paul gathered the disciples, encouraged them, said goodbye, and set out for Macedonia.

f.w: departed for to go into Macedonia

chapters.n: He traveled through Macedonia, strengthening the churches with much encouragement, and then went on to Greece.

f.g: Here, the province of Achaia, including Corinth.

chapters.n: He stayed three months — likely in Corinth, where he probably wrote Romans. Learning of a plot against him, he changed plans and went back overland through Macedonia.

f.g: Plotted, set an ambush.

chapters.n: Paul traveled with a group of representatives from various churches — likely carrying the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem.
These companions went ahead and waited for Paul’s group at Troas.
The “we” returns — Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi. After the Passover season they sailed to Troas in five days and stayed a week.

f.g: The week-long feast following Passover, in spring.

chapters.n: On Sunday, the first day of the week, the believers met to “break bread” — the sacrament. Paul, leaving the next day, preached until midnight.

f.w: the first day of the week

chapters.n: Many oil lamps burned in the crowded upstairs room, making it warm and stuffy — a detail that helps explain what happened next.

f.g: An upstairs room, often used for gatherings.

chapters.n: A young man named Eutychus, sitting in a window, fell asleep during Paul’s long sermon and fell three stories. He was picked up dead.

f.g: A name meaning “fortunate” — fitting, given what follows.
The third story.

chapters.n: Paul went down, lay on him and embraced him, and said, Don’t worry — his life is in him. Like Elijah and Elisha, Paul restored the young man to life.

f.w: fell on him, and embracing him

chapters.n: Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, ate, and kept talking until dawn before leaving.
They took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.

f.g: Greatly — an understatement for emphasis.

chapters.n: Luke and the others sailed ahead to Assos, while Paul chose to walk there — about 20 miles overland — perhaps wanting time alone.

f.g: Intending to go on foot.

chapters.n: They picked Paul up at Assos and sailed to Mitylene on the island of Lesbos.
They island-hopped down the coast past Chios and Samos to Miletus. Luke records the voyage like a careful travel diary.

f.g: A port about 30 miles south of Ephesus.

chapters.n: Paul skipped Ephesus to avoid delays, hoping to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, about fifty days after Passover.

f.g: Jewish harvest festival, fifty days after Passover.

chapters.n: From Miletus he sent for the elders of the Ephesian church to meet him there.
Paul’s farewell speech to the Ephesian elders — the only speech in Acts addressed to Church leaders. He begins by reminding them how he lived among them.
He served the Lord humbly, with tears, enduring trials from plots against him.

f.g: Trials, hardships.

chapters.n: He held nothing back that would help them, teaching both in public and in their homes.
His message to Jews and Greeks alike: turn to God in repentance and have faith in Jesus Christ — the first principles of the gospel.

f.w: repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Now, compelled by the Spirit, Paul was heading to Jerusalem without knowing what would happen there.

f.g: Constrained or compelled by the Spirit.

chapters.n: He knew only that the Holy Ghost warned in every city that imprisonment and suffering awaited him.
But none of that would stop him. His life mattered less to him than finishing his mission joyfully and testifying of God’s grace.

f.w: the gospel of the grace of God

chapters.n: He told them sadly that they would never see his face again.
He solemnly declared himself free of responsibility for anyone’s spiritual loss — he had done his duty.

f.w: pure from the blood of all men

chapters.n: He had not avoided teaching them the whole plan and purpose of God, including the hard parts.

f.g: God’s full plan and purpose.

chapters.n: Paul charged the elders to watch over themselves and the flock, which the Holy Ghost had appointed them to shepherd. The Church is precious — bought with Christ’s own blood.

f.g: Greek episkopoi — overseers, the word later rendered “bishops.”

chapters.n: He warned that after he left, vicious “wolves” would come in and attack the flock — an early prophecy of apostasy.
Worse, some from their own leadership would twist the truth to gain followers. Latter-day Saints see this as foretelling the Great Apostasy.
So stay alert, and remember how for three years I warned you day and night with tears.
Paul entrusted them to God and his gracious word, which can build them up and give them an inheritance among the sanctified.

f.g: Entrust, place in someone’s care.

f.w: an inheritance among all them which are sanctified

chapters.n: He had never wanted anyone’s money or possessions.

f.g: Desired, craved.

chapters.n: His own hands — as a tentmaker — had supported him and his companions.

f.w: these hands have ministered unto my necessities

chapters.n: By working hard he set an example of helping the weak. He quotes a saying of Jesus found nowhere in the Gospels: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”

f.w: It is more blessed to give than to receive
f.g: A saying of Jesus preserved only here.

chapters.n: When he finished, Paul knelt and prayed with them all.
They all wept openly, hugged him, and kissed him goodbye.

f.g: Embraced him warmly.
Wept bitterly.

chapters.n: What saddened them most was knowing they would never see him again. They walked him to the ship.
Tearing themselves away from the Ephesian elders, Paul’s group sailed southeast past the islands of Cos and Rhodes to Patara on the mainland.

f.g: Cos, an island off southwest Asia Minor.
A port in Lycia, on Turkey’s southern coast.

chapters.n: At Patara they found a larger ship crossing the open sea to Phoenicia and boarded it.
They sighted Cyprus, passed it on their left, and landed at Tyre, where the ship unloaded its cargo.

f.g: Came in sight of.
Unload her cargo.

chapters.n: They stayed a week with disciples in Tyre, who, moved by the Spirit, urged Paul not to go to Jerusalem. The Spirit revealed the danger; their love made them want to stop him.
When it was time to go, the whole community — wives and children too — walked them out of town. They knelt on the beach and prayed together.

f.w: we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed

chapters.n: They said their goodbyes, boarded the ship, and the Tyrian believers went home.
They sailed on to Ptolemais (modern Acre), greeted the believers, and stayed one day.

f.g: Modern Akko (Acre), a port in northern Israel.

chapters.n: Next they reached Caesarea and stayed with Philip the evangelist, one of the seven men chosen to serve in Acts 6, who had taught the Ethiopian official.

f.g: One who proclaims the good news; Joseph Smith taught that an evangelist is a patriarch.

chapters.n: Philip had four unmarried daughters who had the gift of prophecy — a reminder that women shared in spiritual gifts in the early Church.
During their stay, the prophet Agabus came down from Judea — the same man who had foretold the famine years earlier.
Agabus acted out a prophecy: he tied his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and said the Jews in Jerusalem would bind Paul and hand him to the Gentiles — just as happened to Jesus.

f.g: A long cloth belt or sash.

f.w: deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles

chapters.n: Everyone — including Luke — begged Paul not to go.

f.g: Pleaded with, begged.

chapters.n: Paul replied, Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I’m ready not only to be bound but to die for the Lord Jesus. The warnings prepared him; they didn’t forbid him.

f.w: ready not to be bound only, but also to die

chapters.n: When he couldn’t be persuaded, they stopped and said, “The will of the Lord be done” — echoing Jesus in Gethsemane.

f.w: The will of the Lord be done

chapters.n: Afterward they packed their belongings and went up to Jerusalem.

f.g: Baggage, things carried — not vehicles.

chapters.n: Some Caesarean disciples came along and took them to stay with Mnason, a believer from Cyprus who had been a disciple from the early days.

f.g: A disciple of long standing, from the beginning.

chapters.n: The believers in Jerusalem welcomed them warmly.
The next day Paul met with James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, and all the elders.
After greeting them, Paul reported in detail what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. He likely also delivered the collection for the poor.

f.g: Reported one by one, in detail.

chapters.n: The leaders praised God but noted a problem: thousands of Jewish believers were still zealous for the law of Moses.

f.g: Devoted to keeping the law of Moses.

chapters.n: These believers had heard rumors that Paul told Jews living abroad to abandon Moses and stop circumcising their children. The rumor was an exaggeration — Paul taught that Gentiles didn’t need these things.
What should we do? They will certainly hear that you’ve arrived.
The elders proposed a plan: four men were completing a vow.

f.g: Probably a Nazarite vow of special devotion to God.

chapters.n: Join them in their purification and pay their temple expenses. That would show everyone that Paul still honored the law and the rumors were false.

f.g: Pay their expenses — the costly offerings that ended a vow.

chapters.n: As for Gentile believers, the council’s earlier decision still stood: only the four basic requirements applied to them.
Paul agreed. The next day he purified himself with the men and went into the temple to announce when their purification would be complete and offerings made.
Near the end of the seven days, Jews from the province of Asia spotted Paul in the temple, stirred up the crowd, and seized him.

f.w: the Jews which were of Asia
f.g: Likely from Ephesus, where they had opposed Paul before.

chapters.n: They shouted that he taught against Israel, the law, and the temple — and that he had defiled the temple by bringing Greeks inside. Gentiles were forbidden beyond the outer court on pain of death.

f.g: Warning inscriptions forbidding Gentiles to enter the inner courts have been found by archaeologists.

chapters.n: Their accusation rested on an assumption: they had seen Paul in the city with Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, and assumed he took him into the temple.
The whole city was in an uproar. They dragged Paul out of the temple, and the gates were immediately shut.
As they tried to kill him, word reached the Roman commander of the garrison that Jerusalem was in chaos.

f.g: A tribune commanding a cohort of about 1,000 soldiers.

chapters.n: The commander rushed down with soldiers and officers, and the mob stopped beating Paul.

f.g: Officers each in charge of about 100 soldiers.

chapters.n: The commander arrested Paul, had him bound with two chains — fulfilling Agabus’s prophecy — and asked who he was and what he had done.
The crowd shouted conflicting things, so the commander ordered Paul taken into the fortress.

f.g: The Antonia Fortress, beside the temple, where Roman soldiers were stationed.

chapters.n: When they reached the steps, the mob was so violent that soldiers had to carry Paul.
The crowd followed, shouting “Away with him!” — the same cry once raised against Jesus.
At the fortress entrance, Paul politely asked to speak — in Greek, which surprised the commander.
The commander had assumed Paul was an Egyptian rebel who had recently led thousands into the wilderness. Josephus also mentions this Egyptian false prophet.

f.g: Greek sikarioi — “dagger-men,” assassins who targeted Romans and their collaborators.

chapters.n: Paul identified himself as a Jew from Tarsus, an important city, and asked to address the people.

f.g: No unimportant city — Tarsus was a respected center of learning.

chapters.n: Given permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned for silence. When the crowd quieted, he spoke to them in their own language — Hebrew or Aramaic.

f.g: Probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea, closely related to Hebrew.

chapters.n: Standing on the fortress steps, Paul respectfully addresses the hostile crowd as family: “Men, brethren, and fathers.” This is the first of his defense speeches in Acts.

f.g: Greek apologia — a formal reply to charges.

chapters.n: When they heard him speak in their own language, the crowd grew even quieter. Speaking to people in their own tongue builds trust.
Paul stresses his Jewish credentials: born in Tarsus but raised in Jerusalem, trained by the famous rabbi Gamaliel in strict observance, and as zealous for God as they are.

f.g: As a student — disciples sat at their teacher’s feet.

chapters.n: He admits he once persecuted “this Way” to the point of death, imprisoning men and women.

f.w: I persecuted this way unto the death

chapters.n: The high priest and council could confirm it — they had given him letters authorizing arrests in Damascus.

f.w: all the estate of the elders
f.g: The whole council of elders — the Sanhedrin.

chapters.n: Near Damascus at midday, a brilliant light from heaven suddenly blazed around him — brighter than the noon sun.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” To persecute the Saints was to persecute Christ himself.
“Who are you, Lord?” The answer: “I am Jesus of Nazareth.” The one Paul thought was dead and cursed was alive and glorified.
His companions saw the light and were frightened but didn’t understand the voice. The Joseph Smith Translation harmonizes Acts 9:7 with this verse.

f.g: The Greek may mean they did not understand the words. JST Acts 9:7 agrees with this verse.

chapters.n: Paul asked what he should do, and the Lord told him to go into Damascus to receive instructions. Humble willingness is the first step of conversion.
Blinded by the glory of the light, Paul had to be led by the hand into the city — the proud persecutor now helpless.
Ananias, a devout, law-keeping Jew respected by the local Jewish community, came to him. Paul highlights this to reassure his Jewish audience.
Ananias called him “Brother Saul” and told him to receive his sight — and Paul could see immediately.
Ananias explained that the God of their fathers had chosen Paul to know his will, see the Righteous One, and hear his voice.

f.g: The Righteous One — a title for the Messiah.

chapters.n: He would be Christ’s witness to all people of what he had seen and heard. A witness testifies from personal experience.

f.w: thou shalt be his witness unto all men

chapters.n: Why wait? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the Lord’s name. Baptism is tied to forgiveness through Christ.

f.w: be baptized, and wash away thy sins

chapters.n: Later, back in Jerusalem, Paul was praying in the temple when he received a vision. He mentions the temple to show his reverence for it.

f.g: In a state of vision or spiritual ecstasy.

chapters.n: The Lord told him to leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people there would not accept his testimony.

f.w: get thee quickly out of Jerusalem

chapters.n: Paul objected: surely people here know how I imprisoned and beat believers — wouldn’t my turnaround persuade them?
He confessed he stood by approving when Stephen was killed, even guarding the killers’ coats.

f.g: Greek martys — “witness.” It came to mean one who dies for their testimony.

chapters.n: But the Lord said, Go — I will send you far away to the Gentiles. This was Paul’s divine commission.

f.w: I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles

chapters.n: The crowd listened until the word “Gentiles,” then erupted: Rid the earth of him — he doesn’t deserve to live! The idea that God sent a mission to Gentiles enraged them.

f.w: Away with such a fellow from the earth

chapters.n: They shouted, tore off their cloaks, and threw dust in the air — signs of fury and outrage.

f.g: A gesture of rage or of protest against perceived blasphemy.

chapters.n: The commander, who probably didn’t understand Aramaic, ordered Paul taken inside and interrogated under flogging to find out what had caused the uproar.

f.g: Questioned under torture with a scourge — a leather whip often weighted with bone or metal.

chapters.n: As they tied him up, Paul calmly asked the centurion: Is it legal to flog a Roman citizen who hasn’t been convicted? It was not.

f.g: Leather straps.

f.w: a man that is a Roman

chapters.n: The centurion hurried to warn the commander: be careful — this man is a Roman citizen.
The commander came and asked directly whether Paul was a Roman citizen. Paul said yes.
The commander said he had paid a large sum for his citizenship; Paul replied that he was born a citizen — a higher status.

f.w: With a great sum obtained I this freedom
f.g: Under Emperor Claudius, citizenship was often obtained through bribes; the commander’s name, Claudius Lysias, may reflect this (Acts 23:26).

chapters.n: The interrogators backed off immediately, and the commander was alarmed that he had even put a citizen in chains.
The next day, wanting to learn the real charges, he released Paul and convened the chief priests and the Sanhedrin, bringing Paul before them.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council.

chapters.n: Looking steadily at the Sanhedrin, Paul declared that he had always lived with a clear conscience before God — even when persecuting Christians, he had sincerely believed he was right.
The high priest Ananias ordered Paul struck on the mouth. History remembers this Ananias as greedy and violent.

f.g: Son of Nedebaeus, high priest about AD 47–59; not the Ananias of Damascus.

chapters.n: Paul shot back: God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You judge me by the law yet break it by ordering me struck. A “whited wall” looks clean outside but is crumbling within.
Bystanders were shocked: You insult God’s high priest?

f.g: Do you insult, verbally abuse?

chapters.n: Paul replied that he hadn’t realized this was the high priest, quoting the law that forbids speaking evil of a ruler. He quickly showed respect for the office, if not the man.

f.g: I did not know.

f.w: Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people

chapters.n: Seeing the council was split between Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul cried out that he was a Pharisee on trial for his hope in the resurrection. He went to the heart of the matter — the risen Christ.

f.w: I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee
the hope and resurrection of the dead

chapters.n: His words split the council into its two factions.

f.g: Sharp disagreement.

chapters.n: Luke explains: Sadducees denied resurrection, angels, and spirits; Pharisees believed in all of them.

f.w: the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection

chapters.n: A loud argument broke out. Some Pharisee scribes defended Paul: maybe a spirit or angel really did speak to him — let’s not fight against God.

f.w: let us not fight against God

chapters.n: The fighting grew so violent that the commander feared Paul would be torn apart, so soldiers pulled him out and took him back to the fortress.
That night the Lord stood beside Paul: Take courage — you have testified of me in Jerusalem, and you must also testify in Rome. In his darkest hour, Paul received divine reassurance.

f.w: so must thou bear witness also at Rome

chapters.n: The next morning, some men swore an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.

f.g: Took an oath calling down God’s curse on themselves if they failed.

chapters.n: More than forty men joined the plot.
They told the chief priests and elders about their oath, seeking their cooperation.
The plan: have the council ask the commander to bring Paul down for more questioning, and the assassins would kill him on the way.

f.g: Before he even arrives.

chapters.n: Paul’s nephew heard of the ambush and went into the fortress to warn him. This is our only glimpse of Paul’s family.

f.g: Paul’s nephew — the only mention of Paul’s relatives in the New Testament.

chapters.n: Paul asked a centurion to take the young man to the commander with important news.
The centurion brought him to the commander, explaining that “Paul the prisoner” had asked for this.

f.g: Asked me.

chapters.n: The commander kindly took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked what he had to say.
The nephew explained the Jewish leaders would ask for Paul to be brought down tomorrow on a pretext.
Don’t agree, he urged — more than forty men have sworn to kill him and are just waiting for your consent.
The commander sent him away with orders to keep the conversation secret.
He ordered a large escort — 200 soldiers, 70 cavalry, and 200 spearmen — to leave at nine that night for Caesarea. God’s promise of protection came through a Roman army.

f.w: the third hour of the night
f.g: About 9 p.m.
Seventy.

chapters.n: He also provided mounts for Paul so he could be delivered safely to Felix, the Roman governor.

f.g: Antonius Felix, governor of Judea about AD 52–59; the historian Tacitus called his rule harsh and corrupt.
Horses or mules to ride.

chapters.n: The commander wrote an official letter to accompany Paul.
Here we learn the commander’s name: Claudius Lysias. He addresses the governor with a formal title of honor.

f.g: A formal title for high-ranking Roman officials; also used of Theophilus in Luke 1:3.

chapters.n: Lysias presents himself well — claiming he rescued Paul because he was a Roman, quietly leaving out that he nearly flogged him.

f.w: having understood that he was a Roman

chapters.n: He explains that he brought Paul before the Jewish council to learn the charges.
His conclusion: the dispute concerned Jewish law, and Paul had done nothing deserving death or prison. Another Roman official declares Paul innocent.

f.w: nothing laid to his charge worthy of death or of bonds

chapters.n: Learning of the plot, Lysias sent Paul on immediately and told the accusers to present their case to Felix.
The soldiers marched Paul through the night to Antipatris, about 35 miles from Jerusalem.

f.g: A military post built by Herod the Great, roughly halfway to Caesarea.

chapters.n: Past the dangerous hill country, the foot soldiers returned to Jerusalem while the cavalry continued with Paul.
At Caesarea they delivered the letter and Paul to the governor.
Felix read the letter and asked Paul’s home province — to decide whether he had jurisdiction. Learning he was from Cilicia, he agreed to hear the case.

f.g: A Roman province including Paul’s hometown, Tarsus.

chapters.n: Felix said he would hold the hearing when the accusers arrived, and kept Paul under guard in the palace Herod the Great had built.

f.g: Herod’s praetorium — the palace that served as the governor’s headquarters.

chapters.n: Five days later the high priest came to Caesarea with elders and a professional lawyer, Tertullus, to press charges against Paul before Governor Felix.

f.g: A professional advocate or attorney skilled in Roman legal speech.

chapters.n: Tertullus opened with lavish flattery, praising Felix for bringing peace and reforms. In reality Felix’s rule was marked by unrest and brutality.

f.g: Peace — Felix had violently suppressed rebel groups.
Foresight, wise administration.

chapters.n: More flattery: we gratefully acknowledge your benefits everywhere, most excellent Felix.
Not wanting to take too much of your time, he said, please kindly hear us briefly.

f.g: Kindness, graciousness.
Tiresome, burdensome.

chapters.n: Tertullus brings three charges: Paul is a public menace, a stirrer of riots among Jews everywhere (a political crime Rome took seriously), and a ringleader of the Nazarene sect.

f.g: A plague, a public nuisance.
Rebellion against authority.
A name for Christians, after Jesus of Nazareth.

chapters.n: The fourth charge: Paul tried to desecrate the temple. They claimed they arrested him to judge him by their law — leaving out that they had been beating him.
Tertullus blames the commander Lysias for using violence to take Paul. Many ancient manuscripts omit the end of verse 6 through the start of verse 8.

f.g: A distorted account — Lysias had rescued Paul from a mob.

chapters.n: If you examine him yourself, Tertullus says, you will confirm our accusations.
The Jewish leaders present joined in, insisting the charges were true.

f.g: Agreed, joined in.

chapters.n: At Felix’s signal, Paul responded — courteously but without flattery — saying he gladly made his defense before someone who had judged this nation for years and knew its customs.
Only twelve days earlier he had come to Jerusalem to worship — hardly time to organize a rebellion.
No one had found him arguing in the temple or stirring up crowds anywhere — not in synagogues or the city.
They have no proof for their charges.
But Paul freely admits one thing: he worships the God of his ancestors according to “the Way,” which they call a sect, believing everything in the law and the prophets.

f.g: Greek hairesis — a sect or party; the same word used for the Pharisees and Sadducees.

f.w: believing all things which are written

chapters.n: He shares their hope in God that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

f.w: a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust

chapters.n: So he strives always to keep a clear conscience before God and people. Paul’s life matches his beliefs.

f.g: A clear conscience, without blame.

chapters.n: After years away, he came to Jerusalem bringing gifts for the poor of his nation and offerings — the collection from the Gentile churches.

f.g: Gifts for the poor.

f.w: to bring alms to my nation

chapters.n: While doing this, he was ritually purified in the temple — not with a crowd or causing trouble — when some Jews from Asia found him.
Those Asian Jews, his original accusers, should be here to make their charges in person. Roman law frowned on accusers who failed to appear.

f.g: Aught — anything.

chapters.n: Or let these men here say what wrongdoing they found when he stood before the Sanhedrin.
Unless, Paul adds pointedly, it was the one thing he shouted: that he is on trial for believing in the resurrection of the dead.

f.w: Touching the resurrection of the dead

chapters.n: Felix, who knew a good deal about “the Way,” postponed a decision until Lysias could come. In practice, he left Paul waiting.

f.g: Adjourned the case.
Your case in full detail.

chapters.n: He kept Paul in custody but with some freedom, allowing friends to visit and care for his needs.

f.g: Serve, help, attend to.

chapters.n: Some days later, Felix and his wife Drusilla — a young Jewish princess, daughter of Herod Agrippa I — sent for Paul to hear about faith in Christ.

f.g: Daughter of Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12) and sister of Agrippa II; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

chapters.n: As Paul spoke of righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and sent him away, promising to listen at a more convenient time. That convenient time may never have come.

f.g: Self-control.

f.w: when I have a convenient season

chapters.n: Felix also hoped Paul would bribe him for release, so he often sent for him and talked with him.

f.g: Conversed, talked.

chapters.n: After two years, Porcius Festus replaced Felix as governor. To please the Jewish leaders, Felix left Paul in prison.

f.g: Succeeded Felix in office (about AD 59).
Paul was held in Caesarea about AD 57–59.

chapters.n: The new governor, Festus, wasted no time. Three days after arriving in the province, he traveled up to Jerusalem to meet its leaders.

f.g: Porcius Festus, governor of Judea about AD 59–62; remembered as more fair-minded than Felix.

chapters.n: Even after two years, the chief priests and Jewish leaders immediately brought up Paul’s case and pressed charges against him.
They asked Festus, as a favor, to transfer Paul to Jerusalem — secretly planning another ambush to kill him on the way.

f.w: laying wait in the way to kill him

chapters.n: Festus refused. Paul would stay in Caesarea, and Festus himself would be returning there soon. Unknowingly, he protected Paul.
He invited their leaders to come down with him and bring charges there, if Paul had done anything wrong.
After a week or so in Jerusalem, Festus returned to Caesarea and the very next day convened court and summoned Paul.

f.g: The official tribunal where a Roman governor gave legal rulings.

chapters.n: The Jewish leaders surrounded Paul and brought many serious accusations — none of which they could prove.

f.g: Serious, heavy.

chapters.n: Paul’s defense was simple: he had committed no offense against Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar.
Wanting to win favor with the Jewish leaders, Festus asked Paul if he would go to Jerusalem for trial before him there.

f.w: willing to do the Jews a pleasure

chapters.n: Paul refused: I’m standing in Caesar’s court, where I should be tried. I’ve done no wrong to the Jews, as you well know.

f.g: The emperor’s court, represented by his governor.

chapters.n: If I deserve death, I won’t try to escape it. But if the charges are false, no one can hand me over to them. Then Paul spoke the decisive words: “I appeal unto Caesar.”

f.g: A Roman citizen’s right to have his case heard by the emperor — at this time Nero.

chapters.n: After consulting his advisers, Festus declared: You have appealed to Caesar — to Caesar you will go. This set Paul on the road to Rome, fulfilling the Lord’s promise.
Some days later King Agrippa and his sister Bernice came to Caesarea on an official visit to welcome the new governor.

f.g: Herod Agrippa II, son of the Herod in Acts 12 and the last of the Herodian kings.
Sister of Agrippa II and of Drusilla (Acts 24:24).

chapters.n: During their long stay, Festus told Agrippa about the prisoner Felix had left behind.

f.g: Left in prison, in chains.

chapters.n: He explained that the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem had demanded a condemnation.
Festus proudly noted that Roman law required that the accused face their accusers and have a chance to defend themselves before any sentence — a principle of justice still valued today.

f.w: have the accusers face to face

chapters.n: So without delay he held the hearing the next day.
But the accusers brought none of the serious crimes Festus had expected.
Instead, they argued about their own religion and about “one Jesus,” who was dead but whom Paul claimed was alive. Without realizing it, Festus summed up the gospel’s central claim.

f.g: Here, religion — a neutral or mildly dismissive term.

f.w: whom Paul affirmed to be alive

chapters.n: Unsure how to handle religious questions, he asked Paul whether he would be tried in Jerusalem.

f.g: Was at a loss about.

chapters.n: But Paul appealed to the emperor, so Festus held him until he could send him to Caesar.

f.g: Here a title — “His Majesty,” the emperor (Nero) — not the earlier emperor Augustus.

chapters.n: Agrippa was curious and said he would like to hear Paul himself. Festus arranged it for the next day.

f.w: I would also hear the man myself

chapters.n: The next day Agrippa and Bernice arrived with great pomp, joined by military commanders and city leaders. Then Paul was brought in — fulfilling Jesus’ words that his servants would testify before kings.

f.g: With great ceremony and display.

chapters.n: Festus introduced the case: here is the man the Jewish people have demanded I put to death, both in Jerusalem and here.
Festus admitted Paul had done nothing deserving death, but since Paul appealed to the emperor, he was sending him.
Festus had a problem: he had nothing definite to write to the emperor. He hoped Agrippa, an expert in Jewish matters, could help after questioning Paul.

f.g: The emperor.

chapters.n: It seemed unreasonable, he said, to send a prisoner without stating the charges. Festus’s embarrassment shows how weak the case against Paul really was.

f.g: Besides, at the same time.

chapters.n: King Agrippa gave Paul permission to speak. Paul raised his hand in the classic gesture of an orator — likely still in chains — and began his defense.

f.g: A customary gesture of a speaker beginning an address.

chapters.n: Paul says he counts himself fortunate to defend himself before Agrippa. His courtesy is sincere, not flattering.

f.g: I consider myself fortunate.

chapters.n: Agrippa was an expert in Jewish customs and debates, so Paul asks him to listen patiently. Paul knows this audience can follow his argument from scripture.
Paul begins with his life story: everyone among the Jews in Jerusalem knows how he lived from his youth.

f.w: My manner of life from my youth

chapters.n: If they were willing, they could testify that he lived as a Pharisee — the strictest party in Judaism.

f.g: The strictest party — the Pharisees were known for exacting observance.

chapters.n: Now he is on trial for his hope in the promise God made to Israel’s ancestors — the coming of the Messiah and the resurrection.

f.w: the promise made of God unto our fathers

chapters.n: All twelve tribes worship God earnestly day and night, hoping to see this promise fulfilled. The irony: Paul is accused for holding Israel’s own hope.

f.g: Earnestly, intensely.

chapters.n: Paul turns to the whole audience: Why should anyone find it unbelievable that God raises the dead? For the God who created life, resurrection is not impossible.

f.w: that God should raise the dead

chapters.n: Paul admits he once felt sure it was his duty to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Sincerity alone doesn’t make someone right.
With the chief priests’ authority, he jailed many saints in Jerusalem and voted for their deaths.

f.w: I gave my voice against them
f.g: Literally “I cast my pebble” — cast my vote against them.
Holy ones — a common name for members of the Church.

chapters.n: He punished believers in synagogue after synagogue, tried to force them to deny their faith, and in his fury chased them to foreign cities.

f.g: Tried to force them to curse or deny Christ.
In a furious rage.

chapters.n: That’s why he was traveling to Damascus with authority from the chief priests.

f.g: Official authorization.

chapters.n: At noon he saw a light from heaven brighter than the sun, shining around him and his companions.

f.w: above the brightness of the sun

chapters.n: They all fell, and Jesus spoke in Hebrew: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.” Fighting God only hurts yourself.

f.g: A proverb: an ox that kicks at the sharp goad driving it only wounds itself.

chapters.n: “Who are you, Lord?” — “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”

f.w: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest

chapters.n: Jesus commanded Paul to stand up: I have appeared to you to make you my servant and witness of what you have seen and what I will yet show you.
The Lord promised to rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles, to whom he was sending him.

f.w: unto whom now I send thee

chapters.n: Paul’s mission in one beautiful sentence: open people’s eyes, turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so they can be forgiven and receive an inheritance among the sanctified.

f.w: sanctified by faith that is in me

chapters.n: So, King Agrippa, I did not disobey that heavenly vision. Joseph Smith later drew strength from Paul’s steadfastness in testifying of what he had seen.

f.w: I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision

chapters.n: He preached first in Damascus, then Jerusalem and Judea, then to the Gentiles: repent, turn to God, and live in a way that shows real repentance.

f.g: Live in ways that fit and prove true repentance.

chapters.n: That is why the Jews seized him in the temple and tried to kill him.
With God’s help he has survived to this day, testifying to everyone — small and great — of only what Moses and the prophets foretold. Paul is preaching fulfillment, not novelty.

f.g: Ordinary people and important people alike.

f.w: the prophets and Moses did say

chapters.n: That the Messiah would suffer, be the first to rise from the dead, and bring light to Israel and the Gentiles.

f.w: the first that should rise from the dead

chapters.n: Festus interrupted loudly: Paul, you’re out of your mind — all your learning has driven you mad! The resurrection sounded absurd to a Roman.

f.g: You are out of your mind.

chapters.n: Paul calmly replied that he wasn’t mad but was speaking true and sensible words.

f.g: Sound-mindedness, good sense.

chapters.n: The king knows about these things, Paul said; none of it happened in secret. Jesus’ ministry, death, and the rise of the Church were public events.

f.w: this thing was not done in a corner
f.g: It happened openly, not hidden away.

chapters.n: Paul pressed Agrippa directly: Do you believe the prophets? I know you do. If he did, he would have to consider their fulfillment in Jesus.
Agrippa responded, “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.” Many read this as a wry deflection — “In such a short time you think you can make me a Christian?”

f.w: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
f.g: The Greek can mean “in a short time,” possibly an ironic dodge.

chapters.n: Paul’s gracious answer: whether it takes short or long, I pray to God that you and everyone here would become as I am — except for these chains.

f.g: Except for these chains — Paul spoke while bound.

chapters.n: With that, the king, the governor, Bernice, and the others rose to leave.
In private, they agreed: this man has done nothing to deserve death or prison.

f.w: nothing worthy of death or of bonds

chapters.n: Agrippa told Festus that Paul could have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar. Yet that appeal was the very path God used to bring Paul to Rome.

f.w: if he had not appealed unto Cæsar

chapters.n: Paul’s journey to Rome begins. He and other prisoners were placed in the care of Julius, a centurion of an imperial regiment. The “we” shows Luke is traveling with Paul.

f.g: The Imperial Cohort — a unit with a title honoring the emperor.

chapters.n: They boarded a ship from Adramyttium, a port near Troas, planning to hug the coast of Asia. Aristarchus of Thessalonica came along as a loyal companion.
The next day they stopped at Sidon, and Julius kindly let Paul visit friends for care. Paul’s character won the trust of his guards.

f.g: Treated kindly.

chapters.n: Contrary winds forced them to sail on the sheltered side of Cyprus.

f.g: Sailed in the lee of Cyprus, sheltered from the wind.

chapters.n: Crossing the open sea along the coast of southern Asia Minor, they reached Myra in Lycia.

f.g: A major harbor for grain ships sailing between Egypt and Rome.

chapters.n: There Julius found an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy and transferred them to it.

f.g: Large grain freighters carried Egyptian wheat to feed Rome.

chapters.n: Progress was slow against the wind. They barely reached Cnidus, then turned south to shelter along Crete, past Cape Salmone.

f.g: The wind not allowing us to go on.

chapters.n: With difficulty they reached a harbor called Fair Havens on Crete’s south coast, near Lasea.

f.g: With difficulty.

chapters.n: Much time had passed, and the season for safe sailing was ending — the Day of Atonement fast (late September or October) was already past. Paul warned them.

f.g: The Day of Atonement; after mid-September Mediterranean sailing grew dangerous, and it largely stopped by November.
Warned, advised.

chapters.n: Paul predicted the voyage would bring disaster — loss of cargo, ship, and possibly lives. His warning came from experience and perhaps inspiration.

f.g: Cargo.

chapters.n: But the centurion trusted the ship’s captain and owner over Paul. Expert opinion was against the prisoner’s advice.

f.g: The pilot or captain.

chapters.n: Fair Havens was poorly suited for winter, so most wanted to push on to Phoenix, a better harbor farther west on Crete.

f.g: Suitable, convenient.
Phoenix, a harbor on Crete — not Phoenicia.

chapters.n: A gentle south wind gave them false confidence. They set sail, staying close to Crete’s shore.
Soon a violent northeaster swept down from the island — a storm sailors called Euroclydon.

f.g: A violent northeast wind; often called the “Euraquilo” or northeaster.
Stormy, violent.

chapters.n: The ship couldn’t face into the wind, so they gave up and let it be driven along.

f.g: Let the ship run before the wind.

chapters.n: Sheltered briefly behind the small island of Cauda, they struggled to haul in the ship’s lifeboat.

f.g: Cauda, a small island south of Crete.
The small dinghy usually towed behind.

chapters.n: They passed ropes under the hull to hold it together and, fearing the sandbars off Libya, lowered the sails and drifted.

f.g: Wrapping cables around the hull to keep it from breaking apart.
The Syrtis — dangerous shoals off North Africa.
Lowered the sail or gear.

chapters.n: Battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship’s gear overboard with their own hands.

f.g: The ship’s rigging and equipment.

chapters.n: For many days they saw neither sun nor stars — sailors’ only means of navigation — and the storm raged on. They gave up all hope of survival.
After they had gone long without food, Paul stood up among them. He gently reminded them they should have listened to him — not to gloat, but to give weight to what he was about to say.

f.g: Going without food — from seasickness, fear, and spoiled supplies.

chapters.n: Now take heart, he said: no one will lose their life — only the ship will be lost.
An angel of the God to whom Paul belonged and whom he served had stood beside him that night.

f.w: whose I am, and whom I serve

chapters.n: The angel said: Don’t be afraid — you must stand before Caesar, and God has granted you the lives of everyone sailing with you. Others were spared because of Paul’s faithfulness.

f.w: God hath given thee all them that sail with thee

chapters.n: So take courage — I trust God that it will happen just as I was told. Paul’s faith becomes an anchor for everyone else.
Still, they would run aground on an island.
On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adriatic Sea, the sailors sensed they were nearing land.

f.g: The central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy, and Sicily — wider than today’s Adriatic Sea.

chapters.n: They took soundings and found the water getting shallower — 120 feet, then 90 feet.

f.g: Measured the depth with a weighted line.
A fathom is about six feet.

chapters.n: Afraid of hitting rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.

f.g: Literally “prayed for day to come.”

chapters.n: The sailors secretly lowered the lifeboat, pretending to set more anchors from the bow, but planning to abandon ship.

f.g: Under pretense.
The bow, front of the ship.

chapters.n: Paul warned the centurion and soldiers: unless these men stay aboard, you can’t be saved. God’s promise still required human cooperation — the sailors’ skill was needed.

f.w: Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved
f.g: Divine promises often work together with human effort.

chapters.n: This time the soldiers listened. They cut the lifeboat’s ropes and let it drift away.
Before dawn, Paul urged everyone to eat — they had gone fourteen days in anxious near-fasting.

f.g: Take food, eat.

chapters.n: Eat for your strength, he said — not a hair of your heads will perish. They would need energy to reach shore.

f.w: there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you

chapters.n: Paul took bread, thanked God in front of everyone, broke it, and began to eat. His calm, grateful example spoke louder than words.
Everyone was encouraged and ate too.
There were 276 people on board — a large grain ship carrying many passengers.
After eating, they lightened the ship further by throwing the wheat cargo overboard, so it would ride higher and get closer to shore.
At daylight they didn’t recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a beach and planned to run the ship ashore there.

f.g: A bay or inlet.

chapters.n: They cut away the anchors, untied the steering oars, raised the foresail, and headed for the beach.

f.g: Ropes that had lashed up the steering paddles.
Hoisted.

chapters.n: They struck a sandbar where currents met. The bow stuck fast while the pounding surf broke the stern apart.

f.w: a place where two seas met
f.g: A sandbar or reef between two currents; traditionally identified with St. Paul’s Bay, Malta.

chapters.n: The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none could escape — they would be punished if prisoners got away.

f.w: lest any of them should swim out

chapters.n: But the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stopped them. He ordered swimmers to jump overboard first and get to land.
The rest followed on planks and broken pieces of the ship — and every one of the 276 reached land safely, just as God had promised.

f.w: they escaped all safe to land

chapters.n: Safely ashore, the survivors learned they had landed on Malta, an island south of Sicily.

f.g: Malta, in the central Mediterranean.

chapters.n: The islanders showed remarkable kindness, building a fire and welcoming everyone out of the cold rain. “Barbarous” simply means they didn’t speak Greek — not that they were savage.

f.g: Non-Greek-speaking people; the Maltese spoke a Punic (Phoenician) dialect.

chapters.n: As Paul helped gather firewood — the great apostle doing humble work — a snake driven out by the heat bit his hand.

f.g: A venomous snake.

chapters.n: The islanders concluded Paul must be a murderer: he escaped the sea, but Justice (perhaps a goddess they revered) would not let him live.

f.g: Greek Dikē — “Justice,” personified as a goddess who punishes the guilty.

chapters.n: Paul simply shook the snake into the fire and suffered no harm — fulfilling Jesus’ promise to his disciples.
They waited for him to swell up or drop dead. When nothing happened, they swung to the other extreme and decided he was a god — as happened at Lystra.

f.w: said that he was a god

chapters.n: Nearby was the estate of Publius, the island’s chief official, who hospitably hosted them for three days.

f.w: the chief man of the island
f.g: An official title — “first man” of Malta — confirmed by inscriptions found there.

chapters.n: Publius’s father was ill with fever and dysentery. Paul prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him — repaying kindness with a priesthood blessing.

f.g: Dysentery.

f.w: laid his hands on him, and healed him

chapters.n: Word spread, and the other sick people on the island came and were healed.
The grateful islanders honored them in many ways and, when they left, supplied everything they needed for the journey.

f.g: Loaded us with supplies.

chapters.n: After three winter months, they sailed on another Alexandrian ship with the twin gods Castor and Pollux as its figurehead — patrons of sailors.

f.g: The “Twin Brothers” of Greek myth, sons of Zeus, believed to protect sailors.

chapters.n: They stopped at Syracuse, the main city of Sicily, for three days.

f.g: A major port on the east coast of Sicily.

chapters.n: Sailing on, they reached Rhegium at the toe of Italy, then with a south wind arrived at Puteoli, a key port near Naples.

f.g: Sailed a roundabout course.
Modern Pozzuoli, near Naples — a major port for Alexandrian grain ships.

chapters.n: At Puteoli they found fellow believers who invited them to stay a week. Then they set out for Rome.

f.g: Members of the Church — the gospel had already reached Italy.

chapters.n: Believers from Rome walked out to meet Paul at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns, about 40 and 30 miles from the city. Seeing them, Paul thanked God and was encouraged.

f.g: Market of Appius, a stop on the Appian Way about 43 miles from Rome.

chapters.n: In Rome, Paul was allowed to live in his own lodging, guarded by a single soldier — a mild form of custody.
Three days later Paul called together the Jewish leaders of Rome. He explained he had done nothing against his people or their customs, yet had been handed over to the Romans.

f.g: Leaders of Rome’s many synagogues.

chapters.n: The Romans had examined him and wanted to release him, since he had done nothing deserving death.
When the Jewish leaders objected, he was forced to appeal to Caesar — not to accuse his own nation.

f.g: Compelled, forced.

chapters.n: That’s why he invited them — he wears this chain because of “the hope of Israel”: the Messiah and the resurrection.
They replied that they had received no letters or bad reports about him from Judea.
But they wanted to hear his views, since this “sect” was spoken against everywhere.
On an appointed day, many came to his lodging. From morning to evening he explained the kingdom of God and tried to persuade them about Jesus from the law of Moses and the prophets.

f.w: out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets

chapters.n: Some were persuaded; others refused to believe — the familiar response throughout Acts.
As they left disagreeing, Paul had one final word, quoting what the Holy Ghost spoke through Isaiah.

f.g: Isaiah, in Greek spelling.

chapters.n: Isaiah’s commission: these people will hear but not understand, look but not see. Hearing without a willing heart doesn’t lead to understanding.

f.w: Hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand

chapters.n: Their hearts have grown dull and they have shut their eyes and ears — otherwise they would turn and be healed. God longs to heal; people close themselves off.

f.g: Grown dull, insensitive — literally “fat.”

chapters.n: Therefore, God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles — and they will listen. This fulfills the pattern of Acts: from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

f.w: the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles

chapters.n: The Jewish leaders left, arguing intensely among themselves. Many ancient manuscripts omit this verse.

f.g: Much debate.

chapters.n: Paul lived two full years in a rented house, welcoming everyone who came. During this house arrest he likely wrote letters such as Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.

f.g: Rented lodging; Paul likely paid his own costs.
About AD 60–62.

chapters.n: Acts ends not with Paul’s death but with the gospel going forward boldly and unhindered in the capital of the world. The story of the Church continues — and invites us into it.

f.w: with all confidence, no man forbidding him
f.g: The final Greek word, akōlytōs, means “unhindered.”
